events.text: Unmyeong's Thread draws you to a terrace where the Lineage of Ash and Morning keeps the dawn. {npc} is lighting the first ray of the day from a dish of embers and does not turn around. {He} says the dawn is late because someone is standing in its light.

choices.text: Step out of the light and praise the ray

effects.log: {npc} turns at last. The ray lands warm on your sleeve, and {he} says that is the right place for it.
You carry the dish along the terrace and not an ember dies. {npc} says grace is mostly carrying.

choices.text: Ask what a dawn god marries for

effects.log: 'For grace,' {npc} says. 'Yours, if you have any.' You are not sure whether that was a test.

events.text: In the halls of the Long Tide the Thread ends at a pool that rises and falls with no moon over it. {npc}, of the old sea gods, sits on its rim and says the Lineage holds a seat at the Heavenly Court and means to keep it, with or without a partner.

choices.text: Say you want the partner, not the seat

effects.log: The pool goes still. {npc} says the tide has not been this quiet in an age.

choices.text: Be honest: the seat matters too

effects.log: {npc} laughs, short and dry. An honest greed, {he} says, is rarer than an honest love.
{npc} dips a hand in the pool and the water spells your name once, then forgets it. Courtship, {he} says, is learning to be remembered.

events.text: The Lineage of the Unlit Lamp keeps its lore in the dark. {npc} meets you with no light at all and asks you to find the chair by thinking about where it would be. They marry a deep mind, and they test for one at the door.

effects.log: You walk straight to it. {npc} lights one small lamp, for you alone, and says it has not done that for a guest.

choices.text: Feel along the wall like anyone would

effects.log: You find it by the shin. {npc} says that too is a kind of knowing, and lights a lamp to look at the bruise.
{npc} says no one has ever admitted that at the door. The lamp comes on, and the real conversation starts.

events.text: The Lineage of the Root counts the harvests of a thousand worlds, and {npc} counts them aloud while pouring you tea, as one might hum. The tea is from a world that no longer exists. {He} wants to know if you can value a thing that is gone.

choices.text: Value it at nothing, and drink

effects.log: You drink slowly. {npc} says that was the right price, which is the whole of the price.

choices.text: Ask which world, and mourn it

effects.log: {npc} tells you its name. No one has asked in ten thousand years, and {his} voice thins on the last word.

choices.text: Ask what the Root pays for a good marriage

effects.log: 'Everything it has,' {npc} says. 'It has a great deal.' You note that this is a warning and an offer.

events.text: The Lineage of the Hidden Star marries level or up, and {npc} receives you on a parapet of dark glass under a sky of the house's stars. {He} points to the dimmest one and says it is the last suitor who tried to impress {him} with rank.

choices.text: Say you have no rank to offer

effects.log: {npc} looks a long moment, then up, and the dim star seems to brighten a very little.
{npc} nods. 'Level,' {he} says, 'or near it.' It is a verdict, not a welcome, but it is a door.
{He} points to none. 'Mine is not up yet,' {he} says. You come back at night, and there it is.

events.text: The Lineage of the Nine Wells keeps wells of mercy, and the Thread has led you to the ninth, where {npc} is drawing water for no one in particular. The Lineage never takes a dark heart. {He} looks into your reflection in the bucket before looking at you.

effects.log: {npc} looks for a long time and sets the bucket down. 'Mercy needs a clear glass,' {he} says. 'Yours is clear.'

choices.text: Confess the one thing you are ashamed of

mem.note: confessed to me at the well

effects.log: The water in the bucket ripples and settles. {npc} says that confessing is how a well fills.
You draw it up clear, and {npc} drinks first from your hand. That is not a small thing in that house.

events.text: The Lineage of the Silent Drum respects only those who fought in heaven, and {npc} receives you in a hall with a single drum, unstruck. {He} says nothing for a long while, then asks where you stood in the last War in Heaven.

choices.text: Tell it true, and what it cost

effects.log: {npc} lifts the drumstick, strikes once, softly. It is the greatest honour the hall has.

choices.text: Say you stood nowhere, and are ashamed

effects.log: 'Shame is a drum too,' {npc} says. 'Not a loud one.' It is not a no.
{He} tells it in six sentences, and the hall goes colder with every one. You listen to the end.

events.text: The Lineage of the Laughing River heals, and {npc} sees a heart demon across a hall before you have taken three steps in. {He} says nothing of it yet. {He} only fills a cup from the river that runs through the floor and asks if you are thirsty.

choices.text: Drink, and say what you carry

mem.note: drank and told me what you carry

effects.log: {npc} laughs, not unkindly, and the river laughs after. 'That,' {he} says, 'is what the cup was for.'
{npc} lets it be. The river runs a little more softly past your feet.
'A heart that wants to be loved and does not ask,' {npc} says. 'Common. Curable. Sit down.'

events.text: At the Festival of the Turning Stars, {npc} finds you under the lanterns of the Court's lower gardens. The Thread between you has gone taut enough to hum. Everyone nearby pretends not to hear it, loudly.

effects.log: The Thread rings the third note, and somewhere a lantern-god laughs and lets the lamps flare.
The hum fades with the distance. {npc} says only, 'You can't walk far from it,' and is not wrong.
Unmyeong does not answer in person. A moth lands on the Thread and spells the word 'patience'.

events.text: An elder of {npc}'s Lineage asks you to the high table and puts a question in front of you: what will you give a house for the honour of joining it? The table waits with folded hands, and {npc} studies the cloth.

effects.log: You name three things you have done, and one you have not. The elder nods at the last one.

choices.text: Bow, and say you have no answer yet

mem.note: had no answer for our eldest

effects.log: A pause long enough to be rude. Then the elder says honesty is not nothing, and passes the wine.

choices.text: Turn the question and ask what the house would give

effects.log: The table stirs. {npc} looks up for the first time, almost smiling.

events.text: {npc} brings you to the edge of the Court where prayers rise from below like heat off stone, and asks you to choose one to answer together. It is a courtship of a kind the gods find hard to speak of. It is a shared small duty.

effects.log: A child asking for a lost goat to come home. You and {npc} send it back together, smiling like fools.
A city asks for rain. You answer it grandly. {npc} says, kindly, that a soul had asked quieter and been missed.
{He} chooses, and you are surprised how little it matters which. You are doing it together.

events.text: A rumour crosses the Court that {npc} is promised to another house. You hear it from three gods before breakfast, each delighted. The Thread in your chest stays calm. That, you realise, is information.

effects.log: {He} says it was a hope of {his} elders, not a promise of {his}. You believe {him}, and the Thread agrees.
Watching teaches you the rumour was false and costs you a week of cool dinners.

choices.text: Go to the other house and ask them

effects.log: The other house is baffled and polite. The rumour dies there, and a god of that house is now fond of you.

events.text: Under the Court's great dome, {npc} asks if you would stay for a century, in a way that does not ask it. A century is a short time for gods. It is the first thing {he} has ever asked for that was not already offered.

effects.log: A century. {npc} lets out a breath {he} did not know {he} was holding, and the dome lights go gold.

choices.text: Say you will stay and see

effects.log: 'See,' {npc} repeats, and grins. 'A god of fate would say that.'

choices.text: Ask what it would cost the Thread

effects.log: Nothing, {npc} says, and then, more truthfully, perhaps everything. You stay anyway.

events.text: A rival god of the Court comes to your door with a gift of a thousand-year-old wine and an invitation to dine, plainly meant to cut across your courtship with {npc}. {npc} is not there. {He} will hear of it, though.

choices.text: Say yes to the dinner, and save the wine for {npc}

mem.note: kept the rival wine for me

effects.log: You dine, and carry the wine home unopened. {npc} laughs until the lanterns shake.
You refuse so sweetly the rival thanks you for it. {npc} hears and is quietly, hugely proud.

choices.text: Send the wine back with a verse

effects.log: The verse is pointed. The rival blushes for a decade, and so does half the Court.

events.text: The Court's heralds ring your union into the Book of Fates, and the pages turn by themselves to a clean leaf. {npc}, your Divine Consort now, takes the pen with {his} left hand and writes one word, a domain, and waits for you to write yours beside it.

mem.note: wrote our domains side by side

effects.log: The two words lie together on the leaf. A thin gold line runs between them, and the whole Court exhales.
Yours sits below. {npc} looks, says nothing, and later moves it up with a fingertip.

choices.text: Ask the heralds to leave the page unsigned until you both are sure

effects.log: The heralds consult the Book. It permits a day, and no more.

events.text: The feast of the union is held on a cloud of both your Lineages, whose elders sit at opposite ends and nod at one another as monarchs of old nodded across a battlefield. {npc} squeezes your hand under the table and whispers that it was this or a war.

effects.log: The elders drink, startled. For one evening the cloud holds no old grudge at all.

choices.text: Whisper back that you would have chosen the war

effects.log: {npc} shakes with silent laughter, and an elder at the far end looks at you suspiciously.

choices.text: Slip away together onto the night terrace

effects.log: The feast goes on without you. Nobody mentions it, and everybody notices.

events.text: On the night after the union the two domains touch for the first time. {npc}'s stirs against yours like a wind finding a shore. For a moment you feel the whole of {his} work in the world below, every small prayer, every answered rain.

effects.log: You feel the work of {npc}, and {he} yours. Neither of you says a word until dawn.

choices.text: Keep a wall between them, for now

effects.log: The domains hum and part. {npc} says gently that walls are allowed. {He} keeps one door open, in case.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to show you the prayer that moved {him} most

effects.log: {He} shows you. It is a small one, and you carry it with you for a long time.

events.text: A child is born to the union, and the infant's first breath stirs a draught in the nursery: the faintest spark of a domain, a God-Touched child. {npc} does not cry. {He} blinks at the lamp, and the lamp gently turns the colour of {his} eyes.

choices.text: Name the child for the spark

effects.log: The name is written into the Book of Fates in small gold. The infant sneezes, and a petal of rain falls on the page.

choices.text: Name the child for a grandparent of the house

effects.log: The elders weep with joy. The spark in the infant dims and brightens, as if listening to be called something else.

choices.text: Cover the lamp and let the child sleep

effects.log: You cover the lamp. The spark goes quiet. It will wake in its own time.

events.text: The midwives of the Laughing River bring {npc} to you in a cloth of morning. Unmyeong's Thread has a loose end now, trailing from the child's wrist, and an old fate-weaver is waiting to ask whether it may be tied to a destiny.

choices.text: Say no: the child ties its own thread

effects.log: The weaver bows, vexed. The loose end curls round the infant's finger and stays, untied.

choices.text: Let the weaver read it, and listen

mem.note: had my fate read at birth

effects.log: The weaver reads, and says nothing aloud, but a corner of the cloth warms in a way that feels like a promise.

choices.text: Ask the weaver for one small blessing only

effects.log: The weaver grants one: that the child will always know the way home. It is a modest gift, and it will matter.

events.text: The newborn {npc} is carried before the altar of your Lineage, and every ancestral lamp flares at once, then dims, one by one, in the order of the old gods who made the house. The last lamp stays lit longest. It belongs to you.

choices.text: Hold the child to that lamp

mem.note: held to the lamp of my parent

effects.log: The lamp leans toward the infant and does not gutter. A very old god of the house wipes an eye.

choices.text: Carry the child out into the daylight instead

effects.log: Daylight is the child's first domain, the elders murmur. It does not look like a grave one, either.

choices.text: Say the child will choose its own altar

effects.log: A scandalised silence, then one small laugh from the back. The house will manage.

events.text: The Heavenly Court seals your Lineage into the Book of Fates, and a hall rises on a cloud of its own: a single long room of pale light, and an altar with nothing on it yet. Your God-Touched kin stand along the walls, waiting for what you will put there.

choices.text: Leave it bare: let the Lineage earn its ancestors

effects.log: The altar stays empty. Your kin understand slowly that it is theirs to fill.

choices.text: Place the first offering ever made to you

effects.log: A clay cup of river water from a village that no longer prays. Every visitor asks, and every one is told.

choices.text: Place a handful of earth from the worlds below

effects.log: A little dust on a light altar. The Lineage will not forget where gods come from.

events.text: A herald of the Court brings the seal of your Lineage and a scroll of what a divine house owes heaven: tribute, a seat in the council of Lineages, and silence about the worlds whose prayers you once answered.

effects.log: The herald bows low. The Lineage has a seat at the council from this day.

choices.text: Accept, except the silence about the worlds below

effects.log: The herald writes it down with a pained face. The first thing you do is turn an ear to the prayers.

choices.text: Accept the seal and return the scroll unread

effects.log: The Court is scandalised for an age. The younger Lineages think it magnificent.

events.text: {npc}, of your blood, has fallen in love with a god of the Hidden Star and wishes to leave the Lineage's halls for the star's. The elders say the Lineage needs {him} here, and look to you.

effects.log: {npc} bows and goes to the Lineage's library. The star-god's letters keep arriving.

choices.text: Let {him} go, and bless the road

effects.log: The elders grumble for a century. {npc} sends a lantern from the star every year.

mem.note: let me go to my star

effects.log: A compromise as clumsy as it is kind. {npc} walks a bridge of cloud between halls for a long time and is happy.

events.text: A cousin of the Lineage has insulted {npc} before the council, and {npc} has asked for a duel of domains. The cousin is older, and the elders mutter. {npc} looks at you, not for permission, but as if wanting a witness.

effects.log: The Lineage keeps its peace, and {npc} keeps a grudge that outlasts the cousin.

mem.note: let me fight my own duel

ok.log: {npc} wins by a breath, and bows to the cousin, and the council falls silent in respect.

mem.note: let me fight my own duel

fail.log: {npc} loses, and is hurt, and thanks you for the chance. The council mutters about your rashness.

events.text: {npc} reaches the edge of a greater divinity and stalls there, as gods of the blood sometimes do. The elders whisper that a rival Lineage has offered a rite to push {him} past it, for a price.

choices.text: Refuse the rite: let {him} climb unaided

effects.log: {npc} climbs for a century more, and breaks through by {his} own strength. Slowly, and gladly.

choices.text: Pay the price and take the rite

effects.log: {npc} rises at once. The rival Lineage rises a little with {him}, and the elders pretend not to notice.

events.text: A rival Lineage proposes that {npc} marry into theirs, to end an old quarrel over the right to a river's faith. The terms are very good for the Lineage and not obviously good for {npc}.

effects.log: The quarrel ends. {npc} is dutiful, and the dutifulness has a coldness in it.
{npc} meets the rival heir three times and chooses someone else entirely. The rival sulks. The Lineage is happier.
The rival is insulted and says so at Court. {npc} thanks you privately, and warmly.

events.text: The council of Lineages meets, and your seat among them is a quiet one. A senior god leans across and says it is time the Lineage spoke on the matter of the worlds' faith: who may take it, who may keep it.

effects.log: You listen, and the council's gratitude is a small, real thing.
You speak plainly. Half the council is shocked and the other half writes it down.

events.text: A prayer rises to the Lineage's altar from a world whose god was unmade long ago: a bare hearth, a rain-bowl, a family asking for anything at all. The altar is the only thing listening.

effects.log: A bowl of rain falls in the cold hearth, and a family below is warm. The Court notes it with a very small pen.

choices.text: Pass it to a younger kinsman

effects.log: The younger god is glad of it, and answers better than you would have. The Lineage grows a little.

events.text: The Lineage's treasury of faith has run thin: three harvests of poor prayer, and an elder has pledged part of next age's tithes to a god of the Root to cover it. The elder is ashamed, and has come to you.

choices.text: Cover the debt from your own faith

effects.log: You pay from your own harvest of prayers. It stings, and the elder will not forget the way you did it.

choices.text: Ask the Root to wait an age

effects.log: The god of the Root is astonished at the cheek, and says yes, for a price in favours.

events.text: {npc}, a kinsman of yours below, an old mortal now, prays to you in a cracked voice by a sick bed. The Court forbids answering a prayer from blood. The prayer rises anyway, through the floor of the sky, to your ear.

effects.log: A fever breaks in a far room. The Court notes the breach in the Book of Fates, in a small, tired hand.

mem.note: sent a miracle when I needed it

choices.text: Keep the Court's rule, and grieve

effects.log: You watch the prayer thin to a whisper and stop. You will remember it.

events.text: {npc}, of your blood below, has fallen into trouble with a magistrate and prays for you to change the verdict. The Thread of fate lies just there, loose and easy to pluck. The Court is watching someone else this age.

effects.log: The verdict softens. Unmyeong's moth settles on your sleeve and says nothing, which is worse.

choices.text: Let the verdict stand, and send comfort

effects.log: A small warmth enters {npc} in the cell. They get through it.

events.text: A descendant of your blood has founded a small shrine to you in a village that has long forgotten why. {npc} lays bread on it every morning and talks to it about the harvest. You have never had so earnest a worshipper.

effects.log: Petals fall on the shrine one morning. The village calls it a miracle and the Court, a misdemeanour.

mem.note: sent a rain of petals on my shrine

effects.log: You listen to every word of the harvest talk. It is the best thing you have heard all age.

events.text: {npc}, of your line, is to be wed in a hill town, and the household has set out a bowl for you at the feast, as custom asks. The bowl sits, steaming, with nobody at it. It is, you feel, the most tender thing you have been offered.

choices.text: Drink from the bowl, from above

effects.log: The steam leans toward the empty seat, and the whole feast goes silent, then roars.

mem.note: drank from the bowl I left

effects.log: A thread of luck falls over the couple. They will never know why.

events.text: {npc}, of your line, is a scholar now, and has written a treatise on the gods that gets nearly everything wrong, and you most of all. It is dedicated to you, in very small letters, with a note asking for a sign.

choices.text: Send a dream with the truth in it

effects.log: {npc} wakes and burns the treatise, then writes it again, righter. The Court calls it an interference.

choices.text: Let it stand, errors and all

effects.log: The book travels the lower worlds, wrong and well loved. There are worse fates for a god.

events.text: A delegation of the Lineage a past life of yours founded waits for you on the cloud road. They have kept your seat swept through all the ages you were gone, and they say they would know your soul in any vessel.

effects.log: They lead you to the hall, the altar, and the first name carved there, which is yours.

choices.text: Bless them and walk on as who you are now

effects.log: The eldest bows low and says the seat will wait. Seats in the Court are good at waiting.

events.text: At the Heavenly Court a young god stops in front of you, stares, and runs. An hour later the whole of the Lineage your past life founded is outside your door in silence, with the ancestral tablet held between them.

choices.text: Open the door and take the tablet

effects.log: The tablet is warm in your hands. Behind you the Lineage rises from its knees, and it is yours again.

choices.text: Ask them to let the old name rest

effects.log: They are quiet a long time, and then the eldest says, 'Then we will keep it for you.' And they go.

events.text: It felt like a single hymn since you took your seat in the Court: one long hearing of the First Hour, a walk on a cloud, a talk with a river-god. Then you lean over the rim and listen, and {fab_years} years have gone by below. The tree you planted by the gate is taller than the roof.

effects.log: You listen until the prayers thin out for the night, as if you could make up the years by hearing hard enough. You cannot. You listen anyway.

choices.text: Close your ear to the lower worlds

effects.log: You close it. A hymn up here, a lifetime down there. You will have to learn to listen in smaller doses.

events.text: You meant to listen for a moment. Up here the moment lasts the afternoon, and below the afternoon is {fab_years} years: {fab_kids} of your blood grown into people you would pass in a market without knowing. One of them prays with a hand behind the back, the way you do.

choices.text: Count them all, one by one

effects.log: You find every one of them and say their names aloud to the empty hall. The hall keeps them.

choices.text: Listen for the one who prays like you

effects.log: You hear that one all afternoon. Whoever they became, the way of standing is still yours.

events.text: From the rim of the Court you hear {npc}, of your blood, praying in the old courtyard at dawn. {He} is past forty now, with lines at the eyes you never saw form. {He} still opens the prayer with the words you taught {him}, when {he} was small enough to stumble on them.

choices.text: Send down a breath of wind

mem.note: felt a wind from the heavens at dawn

effects.log: A soft wind crosses the courtyard below. {npc} stops, looks up, and finishes the prayer with tears on {his} face.
You only listen. {npc} does not need the sky to answer. That is the hardest and best thing the Court teaches.

events.text: {npc} has children of {his} own now. You hear {him} carry the youngest down to the river on {his} shoulders, the way you once carried {him}, and you have to sit down on the Court's step for a while. A hymn up here. A whole childhood down there, and you were not in it.

effects.log: You let a thread of grace fall into the river. Below, the water runs clear and sweet all summer, and nobody knows why.
You turn away from the rim. You will listen again tomorrow, which below is next year.

events.text: {npc}, of your blood, is arguing in a market below, loudly, over the price of salt, with exactly the gesture you used to make at merchants: two fingers raised, then a slow shake of the head. You laugh aloud in the Hall of Hearing. A passing god stops to see what is funny.

effects.log: You explain about the salt, and the fingers, and the child. The god listens, and tells you about a child of their own, long ago.
'Nothing,' you say. It is not nothing. It is the best thing you have heard in a thousand years.

events.text: {npc} is old. You tune your ear and there it is: a cough, a cane tapping, an old voice praying beside a plum tree you planted the year {he} was born. {He} prays there every evening now, looking up. The neighbours think {he} is watching the weather.

effects.log: You will go down once before the end. It will cost you at the Court. You do not care what it costs.
You tell yourself there is time. There always seems to be time, in heaven.

events.text: {npc} has grown older than you ever were as a mortal. You do the sum twice to be sure. Below, {he} teaches a grandchild to hold a brush, guiding the small hand with {his} own, which shakes. Your hands up here are as steady as the sky, and that seems suddenly unjust.

mem.note: felt my hand steadied by something

effects.log: You send the smallest breath of grace. The old hand stops shaking long enough to finish the stroke. {npc} looks at it, puzzled, and smiles.
You let it shake. The stroke is crooked and the grandchild loves it anyway. Some things should not be mended from the Court.

events.text: The physicians below visit {npc} more often now. You count the visits through the rim of the Court, and hate counting them. An old god on the next seat sees your face and says, unasked: 'Go down. I never did. Go down.'

effects.log: The old god only nods and looks away, down through a gap of their own, at nothing anymore.
'Nothing happened,' the god says. 'That is what happened.' You do not need to hear more.

events.text: You come down the Court's last step for one day. {npc} is on the bench under the plum tree, and stands so fast the cane falls, and says your name as if {he} had never stopped saying it. You look younger than your own child now. Neither of you cares.

mem.note: sat with me until dark, one last time

effects.log: You sit under the plum tree and talk until dark, about nothing and everything, and {npc} holds your hand the whole time.

mem.note: brought the whole house out to meet them

effects.log: {npc} calls the whole house out. A dozen strangers of your blood bow to you, wide-eyed. The smallest asks if you can make it rain.

events.text: 'I knew you would come,' says {npc}, who did not know, and has told everyone {he} knew, for forty years. {His} house is small and clean and full of the things you left: your old cup, your handwriting on a chart of the seasons, framed.

mem.note: saw the old cup lifted one more time

effects.log: You take it down and drink from it, for {npc}, slowly. {He} watches as if memorising a rite.

mem.note: was listened to, all day, by someone from heaven

effects.log: You ask, and listen all day: a marriage, a trade, a flood survived, a hundred small brave things. You were not there. Now you know.

events.text: At the end of the one day, at the foot of the Court's stair, {npc} will not let go of your sleeve. Then {he} does, finger by finger, as {he} let go of your hand on the first day of school, a lifetime ago. 'Go on,' {he} says. 'Do not look back. I will be fine.'

effects.log: You do not look back. It is the last thing {npc} asks of you, and you give it.
You look back once from the first cloud. {npc} is waving with both arms, like a child. You will keep that forever.

events.text: Below, a small procession of white banners winds up the hill behind the old house. It is {fab_name}'s. Up here you were only at the First Hour for a season. You kneel at the rim and light one stick of incense, and the smoke goes up instead of down, which is the wrong way for a god to grieve.

choices.text: Follow the procession to the grave

effects.log: You watch the whole funeral from the Court, to the last shovel of earth, and then a while longer.
You send a soft rain over the hill, just there, just then. The mourners say heaven weeps with them. It does.

events.text: You meant to go down. You told yourself there was time, and in heaven there always seems to be. Now the white banners climb the hill below for {fab_name}, the bench under the plum tree is empty, and the visit you meant to make is something you will carry through a very long life.

effects.log: You carry it. Some gods say a regret is a weight that makes the next climb stronger. You hope they are right.

choices.text: Go down to the grave now

effects.log: You go down the Court's stair anyway, too late, and kneel at the fresh grave in the rain, and say what you meant to say.

events.text: {fab_name} is gone. You said goodbye at the foot of the Court's stair, and you did not look back, or you did, and either way it was said. The banners climb the hill. You find you can watch them without looking away, and that this, too, is something the last visit gave you.

choices.text: Light incense and let it go

effects.log: You light one stick and let it burn down, and let the grief go up with the smoke. Not all of it. Enough.

choices.text: Watch over the house left behind

effects.log: You turn your ear from the grave to the house below, full of people of your blood. Someone has to listen now.

events.text: {fab_grand}, of your line below, born after you rose, kneels at the family shrine where your name is carved, faded now, and prays to you very seriously for help with an examination. They have never heard your voice. They are quite sure you are listening.

effects.log: That night you send a dream down: an old courtyard, a brush, a stance. {fab_grand} wakes up certain.
A white bird lands on the shrine roof and stays a whole morning. {fab_grand} decides that counts.
You stay silent. Whatever they do, they should do it themselves. You find you are proud of them already.

events.text: {fab_grand} does not believe in you. You hear it through the floor of heaven, at a feast below: the ancestor who rose to be a god is a story, a thing grandparents say to make children eat their vegetables. The whole table laughs. An old aunt at the end of it does not.

effects.log: Every teacup on the table below rattles at once. Nobody laughs after that. {fab_grand} looks up.
You let them laugh. A story that makes children eat their vegetables is not the worst thing to have become.

events.text: Someone is climbing the mountain below: {fab_grand}, of your line, with a pack and a borrowed staff, determined to find the altar of the famous ancestor and see the god with their own eyes. It is a long way. They are not nearly strong enough. They are climbing anyway.

effects.log: You send a dream of the safe path around the cliffs. {fab_grand} takes it, lives, and turns back at the snow line, wiser.

choices.text: Let them find their own way

effects.log: You let them climb. They turn back at the snow line on their own, bruised and stubborn and alive.

events.text: Below, {fab_grand} is getting married in the old courtyard, and at the head of the table, as is the custom, a seat has been left empty for the ancestor in the heavens. Nobody expects it to be filled. They set a cup of wine there anyway, and bow to it.

effects.log: You reach down, and below, the wine in the cup on the empty seat suddenly shines like dawn. The whole wedding goes silent, then roars.
You send down a single thread of good fortune and say nothing. The couple will be lucky, and never know why.

events.text: The hall of your Lineage keeps a book of the divine blood, every name in gold. Your line below is not in it. The scribes of the Court say the worlds below keep their own records. Looking at the gold names and then down through the floor at {fab_kids} of your blood, you find you disagree.

choices.text: Write the line below into the book

effects.log: You write every name below into the Lineage book in your own hand, in ink, not gold. The scribes are scandalised. You sleep well.

choices.text: Ask the Court for leave to bless below

effects.log: You petition the Court in person, properly, to bless your line below again. Surprisingly, it is granted.
The heavens and the worlds below have their own books. Perhaps that is a mercy for both.

events.text: One of the God-Touched heirs born in heaven asks you at the evening meal whether it is true that there are others of your blood below, mortals, who grow old and die in a few decades. The heir is curious, not unkind. The rest of the Lineage has gone very quiet to hear your answer.

effects.log: You tell them everything: the house, the plum tree, {fab_kids} below. Nobody at the table eats until you are finished.
You take the heir to the rim and open the hush. The heir listens a long time and asks to go down one day. The Court will not like it.

events.text: {npc}, born among the gods and wed to you in the Book of Fates, has never known anyone who grows old. {He} finds you at the rim again, listening, and sits beside you. 'Tell me about them,' {he} says. 'The ones down there. I want to know whom I am sharing you with.'

mem.note: was told about the children below

effects.log: You tell {npc} about every one of them. {He} listens to the end, then asks the names again so as not to forget them.
You open the hush and let {npc} hear the old house, the bench, the plum tree. {He} is quiet a long time. 'They pray like you,' {he} says.

events.text: 'When they are gone,' {npc} asks carefully, one night in the Court, 'the whole line below, will you still listen?' It is not a jealous question. {He} is wed to a god who was once mortal, and is trying to understand what that means.

mem.note: was told the listening would never stop

effects.log: 'Always,' you say. 'Someone will be down there.' {npc} nods, and from then on sometimes listens with you.
'I do not know,' you say. {npc} takes your hand. 'Then we will find out together,' {he} says.

events.text: There is no witness but the first light. {npc} stands across from you on the Court's eastern step and says the old words that Twin Domains have said since the world was young: two domains, one motion, and whoever rises first waits. Then {he} adds, in {his} own voice: 'And no going on alone. Promise.'

effects.log: You promise. The dawn comes up with both domains lit at once, which the old books say is lucky.

choices.text: Promise to wait, not to never leave

effects.log: 'I will wait,' you say. 'I cannot promise more than I know.' {npc} thinks, and accepts the smaller true thing.

events.text: You swear the vow with {npc} in the Court's vestibule, and by the time the first light is out the whole of heaven knows. Supper is very quiet. Someone sets the cups down a little too hard. {npc} reaches for your hand under the table and squeezes it once, which helps, and does not help at all.

effects.log: You say that a vow of domains takes nothing from the house. Nobody answers. But somebody passes the wine.
You eat in silence. Tomorrow will be easier, or it will not; tonight is for the vow.

events.text: You come out of the rising with the world sharper than before, and the first thing you feel is not your own power but {npc}'s: down the thread of the vow, {his} domain stirring in answer, like a second bell struck by the first.

effects.log: You find {npc} on the terrace with {his} eyes closed, breathing the way you breathed an hour ago. You sit beside {him} and keep watch.
You sleep a day and a night. When you wake, {npc} has left a cup of warm milk and a note: Felt it. Well done.

events.text: You rise, and a heartbeat later something in {npc} gives way too, a step behind you on the same stair. The two of you look at one another across the room with the same astonished face. The books say a vow is a thread. Nobody said it would pull.

effects.log: You both laugh at nothing, at everything. The servants of the Court think you have gone mad. Perhaps you have.
You write down exactly what you felt. One day another pair will swear this vow and need to know.

events.text: {npc} rises in the night, and you wake before {he} does, sitting straight up in the dark with your heart pounding and your domain full of someone else's light. It fades by morning. But you know a little more of the next stair than yesterday.

effects.log: {npc} listens with {his} chin in {his} hand. 'So that is what it looks like from outside,' {he} says.
You keep it to yourself. Some things are better as a secret you share without saying.

events.text: {npc} comes out of retreat a rung above where {he} went in, and stands in the doorway blinking at the light like someone who has slept an age. Then {he} looks at you and says, slightly embarrassed: 'I think I left a door open behind me. Come and see.'

effects.log: You sit where {npc} sat. Something of the path is still in the air there, like warmth in a chair.
You make {npc} eat and sleep. The door stays open a little longer than it would have. That seems right.

events.text: The first form of your paired working is nothing at all: you sit back to back with {npc} and learn to move your domains at the same breath. It takes a year. On the last day a sparrow lands on your shoulder, then on {npc}'s, as if it cannot tell which of you is which.

effects.log: You keep it up long after the sparrow has gone. Neither of you wants to be the first to stop.
You call it the Sparrow's Mistake. {npc} groans. The name sticks anyway.

events.text: Halfway through the paired working you stop being able to tell whose rain is whose. {npc} turns a gale that you were about to turn, and you answer a thunder {he} had not yet called. The two of you stand in the weather you made and say nothing.

effects.log: 'Luck,' you say. {npc} raises one eyebrow, and the next gale comes exactly when you wanted it.
You say it. {npc} lets out a breath, and a small bright cloud forms over the two of you.

events.text: The paired working is finished. You know it the way one knows a song is finished: nothing is left to add. {npc} closes {his} hands and the weather closes with them. 'Again?' {he} says, and you laugh, and do it again.

effects.log: You do it again, slower, for pleasure. The Court's gardens bloom out of season, and no one complains.

choices.text: Teach it to a young pair

effects.log: You teach it to a young pair of gods in love. They get it wrong in three delightful ways.

events.text: A season in the quiet with {npc}, the doors of the retreat sealed, one lamp between you. You do not speak for weeks. Your domains fold together like sleeping birds. On the last day {npc} says only: 'Good.'

effects.log: You sit on the step in the light for a whole day, saying nothing. It is the best day of the age.
'All of it,' {npc} says. You do not ask more, and the light holds.

events.text: In the third month of the retreat {npc} speaks, softly, for the first time: a question about the day you first met, and whether the Thread had already tied itself, or was tied by a later choice. You find you do not know the answer.

effects.log: 'Nor do I,' {npc} says. 'It is nice to not know with someone.'
You do not answer. Some questions are better as company than as answers.

events.text: In the dark of the retreat your domain turns all at once, like a river jumping its banks. You are too deep to hold it. {npc} does not hesitate; {he} puts both hands to you and takes the overflow into {his} own.

effects.log: 'You would have done the same,' {npc} says, and then, because {he} is honest: 'I hope.'
If your domain had pulled {him} in, you would both have been unmade. 'I know,' {npc} says, and says nothing else.

events.text: The deviation is {npc}'s this time: in the lamp light you see {his} face go grey and {his} domain start to leak out at the edges like water through a split bowl. You have one breath to choose between two ways of helping.

effects.log: You hold steady. In the morning {npc} opens {his} eyes and says your name, and you start breathing again.

choices.text: Break the seal and run for a healer

effects.log: You break the seal. A healer of the Laughing River comes; {npc} lives. Later {he} asks, quietly, why you did not trust the vow.

events.text: A rumour comes to the house, the kind with a sharp end: {npc} was seen at the Court's lower stair with a stranger, at night, close. You turn the rumour over like a coin and cannot decide which side it will land on.

effects.log: 'A healer,' {npc} says. 'For a cough I did not want you to worry about.' It is true. You are both ashamed, differently.
You say nothing. {npc} knows something is wrong and cannot find out what. A week of cold dinners follows.

events.text: {npc} has found a scroll: half of a working of the old gods, the kind that could carry one of you a rung higher and leave the other where they stand. {He} lays it on the table between you and does not touch it.

effects.log: You push it across. {npc} looks at it a long time, tears it carefully in two and hands you half. 'We learn it together, or not at all.'
You take it. {npc} says nothing. You learn it alone, and it is a good working, and it tastes of ash.

events.text: {npc}, another consort of the house, finds you alone in the corridor of the Court and does not move aside. 'You swore a Twin Domain with someone else,' {he} says. 'I only want to know where that leaves the rest of us.'

effects.log: You tell {npc} in plain words what {he} is to you, which is not the vow but is not less. {He} listens to every word.

choices.text: Say the vow is not for discussion

effects.log: 'The vow is the vow,' you say. {npc} steps aside. The house is very cold for an age.

events.text: {npc} has begun to rise at dawn, hard, alone, on the far terrace where you cannot help seeing. It is not for the domain. It is to be seen being strong. Your Twin Domain hums somewhere behind you, and you feel every note of the quarrel in it.

effects.log: You rise until the sun is high. You say nothing about vows. Afterwards {npc} laughs for the first time in a season.
'You are hurting yourself,' you say. 'Yes,' says {npc}. 'I noticed that too.' {He} does not stop.

events.text: You have gone two rungs past {npc} now, and it shows in everything: {he} cannot follow your weather, cannot hold the second note of the working, and has begun to apologise for it. The apologies are the worst part.

effects.log: 'I swore to wait,' you say. 'I will.' {npc} weeps, then, for the first time in your union, quietly, into your shoulder.

choices.text: Say the Court will not wait for either of you

effects.log: 'The Court does not wait,' you say, kindly. {npc} nods, and says nothing, and begins to train in the dark.

events.text: You are two rungs behind {npc} now. {He} slows when you walk together, shortens {his} stride, pretends not to. At the Court's gate you see {him} glance back to check that you are still coming, and the look on {his} face is pure fear.

effects.log: 'Go at your own pace,' you say. 'I will catch up.' {npc} looks at you a long time and lengthens {his} stride, a little.

choices.text: Say you will not catch up

effects.log: 'I may not,' you say. {npc} stops walking altogether. The gate is very quiet.

events.text: A rung is nothing, said the old gods, and two rungs a different weather. You stand at the lower step of the vestibule of the Court and watch {npc} at the top. The distance is no longer in the stairs. It is in how long you take to answer each other.

effects.log: You and {npc} set a pace, an hour at a time, and it is slow, and it is yours.

choices.text: Let each take the road alone for a while

effects.log: You each go your way. You write letters in the rain, and meet at the equinox.

events.text: {npc} has turned back to wait for you more often than a god of a rising house should. You see the elders noting it. It is a kindness, and a danger, and neither of you has said a word about it.

effects.log: 'Go,' you say. {npc} goes, a little, and returns by evening with a stone from the higher stair, as a gift.
{npc} stays, and talks, and the elders have more to write that night.

events.text: One morning you stand beside {npc} at the edge of the Court's terrace and feel the same weather {he} feels, the same faint pull of the next stair. Neither of you is ahead. Neither of you says anything about it. {npc} just hands you your cup, the way {he} used to, before.

effects.log: You rise together until noon, and it is exactly like before, and better.
'I did not wait,' {npc} says. 'I walked slowly. That is different.' You decide it is not, and say so.

events.text: The gap has closed. You do not feel it at once; you feel it at the second note of the working, which for the first time in years comes from both of you, evenly, like a two-voiced chime. {npc} laughs, and the Court's bells answer.

effects.log: You ring it again, and again, till every bell in the Court is humming. It is a nice kind of nonsense.
You hold it. Some mornings are meant to be kept whole.

events.text: You hand {npc} back the half of the Twin Vow you swore on, or {he} hands you yours; afterwards neither of you can remember which. The union stands. The motion does not. {npc} says only: 'I hope the next rung is worth getting to alone.'

effects.log: You say it. It is the truest thing either of you has said in months, and the coldest.

mem.note: was told the next rung was worth it

effects.log: You say nothing. {npc} nods as if you had, and goes inside.

mem.note: got no answer at the end of the vow

events.text: The vow comes loose between you like a knot that was never really tied. {npc} notices it before you do, and lays {his} hand flat on the table as if to hold the room together. 'We can still be kind,' {he} says. 'That does not need a vow.'

effects.log: You agree. The vow is gone, and the kindness is still there, with a faint sound like rain on a roof.
You say it. {npc} bows, and goes, and the house is quiet for a long age.

events.text: {npc} is at the top of the Court's stair, exactly where the vow said {he} would be. {He} has kept a seat for you on the terrace, and the cup on it is still warm, as if {he} knew the hour. 'You were long,' {npc} says. 'I did say not to be long.'

effects.log: You sit. The clouds go gold beneath you. Neither of you says anything for a long while, and nothing needs saying.
'I am here now,' you say. 'Then we can begin,' says {npc}, 'the next part of the road.'

events.text: You waited in the Court so long that waiting became a kind of rising, and now {npc} comes up the great stair, out of breath, older and somehow younger, and stops two steps below as if not quite sure you are real. You hold out your hand, the way you did once on a ledge above a gorge.

effects.log: You pull {npc} up the last two steps. 'You kept the seat,' {he} says. 'I kept the seat,' you agree.
You let {npc} climb the last two by {his} own strength, because that was the vow too. {He} reaches the top laughing.

events.text: {dcp_name} is gone. The Twin Vow does not say what to do now; the old books are silent on it, as if nobody who swore it ever lived long enough to ask. You find the half of the vow in a drawer, still faintly warm, and you sit holding it until the light goes.

choices.text: Walk the road alone, for both

effects.log: You will walk it for both of you, then. Every step from now on counts double, or it does not count at all.
You lay it at the place where {dcp_name} was last seen. The vow goes where {dcp_name} went. You will have to find your own reasons now.

events.text: The weather you made together is gone from the world, and you feel its absence in every sky. A passing child below asks why the rain is so plain these days. You tell her, in a dream, that it is missing someone. {dcp_name} would have laughed.

choices.text: Make the rain yourself, as well as you can

effects.log: You make it. It is plainer than theirs, and it is yours, and the child below says it smells like home.

choices.text: Let the sky stay plain for an age

effects.log: You let it. Some gaps should be left open for a while, out of respect.

events.text: In heaven a year is nothing; an age is a long afternoon. Below, {dcp_name} is still climbing. You keep a seat for them at the edge of the Court's terrace, and every so often you listen down through the prayers, though you know you will not find them, and come back and sit.

effects.log: You keep it. The other gods have learned not to sit in it. One of them leaves a cup of tea there, now and then.
You send a dream down: a stair, a terrace, a seat. Whether it arrives, you cannot know.

events.text: A god of the Court asks you, kindly, why you never take a new consort here, where there are so many who would. You try to explain about {dcp_name}, and a vow, and the great stair, and find you have been talking for an hour. The god has stopped asking and started listening.

effects.log: You finish it. The god bows to you, deeply, and goes away, and does not ask again.
You stop and laugh. 'It is a long road,' you say. 'I am only halfway through telling it.'

events.text: At the Convocation of the Four Pantheons you are seated beside {npc}, a god of a rival pantheon whose people do not shake hands or give names lightly. {He} offers you a pinch of {his} own pantheon's salt instead, which you realise is a very large thing to offer.

choices.text: Take the salt and eat it

effects.log: The salt is bitter and clean. {npc} watches you swallow it and lets out a small, astonished laugh.

choices.text: Offer salt of your own pantheon in return

effects.log: Your pantheon has no custom of salt, so you give a bit of dawn-light in a cup. {npc} drinks it solemnly.

choices.text: Decline politely and ask about their gods

effects.log: {npc} accepts the refusal gracefully and answers questions for two hours, as if it were its own sort of gift.

events.text: In the year since, {npc} has written to you three times in the formal script of {his} pantheon, each letter ending with a line you cannot read. The Court's scribes cannot read it either. They are not sure it is not a curse.

effects.log: 'It says: I am here,' {npc} writes back. 'It is only that. It is every letter.' You answer in kind.
It takes a year. The first thing you write is the line. {npc} replies in your pantheon's script, badly and with great care.

choices.text: Let the Court scribes keep puzzling

effects.log: The Court's scribes publish a monograph on the line. It is wrong in six places and delights both of you.

events.text: The elders of both pantheons learn of the letters in the same week and say, in the same breath, that it cannot be allowed. {npc} meets you at the border of the two halls, between the pillars, where neither pantheon claims the floor.

effects.log: {npc} is silent for a breath, then bows in the manner of {his} people, which is a very low bow indeed.

choices.text: Say the two of you could make a third rite

effects.log: 'A third rite,' {npc} says slowly. 'Nobody has made one in ten thousand years. I would be glad to be first.'

choices.text: Say it cannot be allowed, and you agree

effects.log: You agree, regretfully, under the pillars. {npc} nods and goes back to {his} hall. The letters stop.

events.text: The wedding is held in the border hall, in the rite of {npc}'s pantheon, with a quiet nod from your own elders at the back who came to see it fail and stayed to see it done well. The salt is passed round. The names are given.

choices.text: Take the vow as the rite asks

mem.note: wed me in my own rite

effects.log: The names are given at last, one by one, and {npc} lets you say {his} first. The hall exhales.

choices.text: Ask {him} to take yours as well

effects.log: Both rites are spoken in one long evening. The elders of both pantheons find themselves holding hands, appalled.

events.text: You and {npc} write the third rite over a hundred years: a salt, a dawn-light, a name given half and half. The Court nods at it, warily. Both pantheons borrow it within the age, each swearing it was their own idea.

mem.note: wed me in a rite we made

effects.log: A rite older than its makers by the time the vows are done. The salt and the light mingle in one cup.

choices.text: Keep it as a promise, not a marriage

mem.note: kept our rite as a promise

effects.log: You do not wed. You keep the rite and renew it each century, which {npc} says is better, and means.

events.text: The Festival of the Heavens comes round once an age, and for one night every god of every rank may dance in the same hall. {npc} crosses it in a robe of stars, straight toward you, and asks if you remember how to waltz a sky.

choices.text: Say you do, and lie badly

ok.log: You remember it halfway through. {npc} leads without seeming to, and the hall turns with you.

mem.note: danced a sky with me, badly

fail.log: You step on a constellation. {npc} laughs and steers round it, and the stars rearrange to help.

choices.text: Say you never learned, and ask to be shown

effects.log: {npc} shows you the first figure slowly, one hand at your elbow, and the hall pretends not to watch.
You watch the whole hall turn, and {npc} dances with half the Court and looks up at you at every turn.

events.text: A year later the Court's heralds announce that the Festival has a secret custom: every pair that danced the first figure is called back to the hall to light one star between them. {npc} is waiting beside the cold lamp, a little shy.

effects.log: The star kindles between your two hands. It will burn a hundred ages, the heralds say, whatever becomes of you.

choices.text: Let {npc} light it alone, and watch

effects.log: {npc} lights it with a breath. 'It is yours too,' {he} says, and puts it in your pocket.
You leave before the lamp is lit. {npc} lights it anyway, alone, and it is a small star, and a sad one.

events.text: On the next night of the Festival you find a note in your sleeve: 'The roof of the Hall of Hearing, midnight.' You go. {npc} is there, and the star you lit is hung over the rooftops, bright, listening to the prayers of a hundred worlds with you.

effects.log: {npc} says it back. The star flares, and somewhere below a hundred prayers for lovers are answered at once.

choices.text: Say you are glad to be here

mem.note: was glad to be on the roof

effects.log: 'That is enough,' {npc} says, 'for tonight.' You sit till dawn, under the star, saying nothing.

choices.text: Say you will return next Festival

effects.log: {npc} smiles and nods. Next Festival is an age away. It is a long time to be kept waiting.

events.text: Two pantheons have fought for a thousand years over a river's faith, and the Heavenly Court has found a way to end it: a union between a god of each. You are named, and so is {npc}, who is as appalled as you. The heralds wait for your answers.
events.arc: A Match to End a War

effects.log: {npc} lets out a breath. 'We will hate it together, then,' {he} says. It is almost a joke.

choices.text: Demand a year to know {him} first

mem.note: asked for a year to know me

effects.log: The heralds grumble, then grant it. {npc} looks at you for the first time as a person.
The heralds are scandalised. The war goes on another decade, and {npc} sends you a note of thanks and sorrow.

events.text: The two of you are seated for the first dinner under the eyes of both pantheons. Neither of you may speak first, by protocol. {npc} lifts the lid of a dish and sighs: it is the one food your people cannot stand and {his} people revere.
events.arc: A Match to End a War

ok.log: You eat it without a flicker. {npc} stares, then takes a bite of yours. The room breathes out.

fail.log: You turn a shade of green. {npc} calls it a draw and laughs so much both pantheons turn.

effects.log: {npc} says that is a relief, and slides {his} own half of it onto your plate when nobody is looking.
You say something small and kind about the river. The room goes silent, then someone laughs, then everyone.

events.text: A faction of {npc}'s pantheon, who want the war to continue, sends an envoy to sow a rumour: that you wed only to take the river. The rumour reaches {npc}. {He} comes to you quite pale.
events.arc: A Match to End a War

choices.text: Show {him} the treaty and the empty clause

effects.log: You show {him} every clause, including the one that gives the river to neither of you. {npc} reads it twice and closes it.
You wade in to the knee and swear. The river, which has heard a thousand years of oaths, goes quiet to listen.

choices.text: Ask the envoy to repeat it before both pantheons

effects.log: The envoy cannot. The faction is shamed, and the rumour dies where it was born.

events.text: The war ends on a morning of cold rain, with a white banner raised on the river bank by both sides at once. {npc} stands beside you for the heralds' reading, and when they come to the clause of the union, {he} takes your hand without being asked.
events.arc: A Match to End a War

mem.note: wed me in earnest after a treaty

effects.log: What began as a clause becomes a marriage. The river rises a little in the rain, as if pleased.

choices.text: Keep the treaty and the friendship, not the marriage

mem.note: kept the peace but not the vow

effects.log: The heralds are baffled, then charmed. The two of you are named Friends of the River, and nothing else.

events.text: A god of a crossroads shrine, very minor, sweeps your steps at the Court one morning when nobody has told {him} to. {npc} gives {his} name when asked, with no lineage after it. The Court's ushers wince. The step is very clean.
events.arc: A Lesser God Courting Above Their Station

effects.log: {npc} blushes to the ears. 'No one up here learns the name of the person with the broom,' {he} says.

choices.text: Ask what a crossroads god sweeps for

effects.log: 'For the pilgrims who come up this stair,' {npc} says. 'It is my whole domain, you see. A clean place to start.'

choices.text: Nod and let the ushers hurry {him} off

effects.log: {npc} is gone in a moment. You regret the nod all day.

mem.note: let the ushers hurry me off

events.text: {npc} has taken to leaving small gifts at your door: a pebble from a road, a feather from a pilgrim's hat, a worn prayer-slip. Gods of rank at the Court notice and begin to smile at you, unkindly, behind their cups.
events.arc: A Lesser God Courting Above Their Station

choices.text: Wear the pebble where they can see it

mem.note: wore my pebble at the Court

effects.log: A murmur crosses the hall. A very old god, not smiling, nods you a quarter of an inch. {npc} hears of it by evening.

choices.text: Keep the gifts private, and write back

effects.log: You write a letter every week. {npc} reads each one three times on a milestone, by moonlight.

choices.text: Ask {him} to stop, for both your sakes

effects.log: {npc} stops. The gifts stop. The step is dirty for a month.

events.text: The elders of your Lineage summon you and tell you plainly that a crossroads god cannot be taken as a consort without diluting the house. {npc} is waiting in the vestibule, hat in hands, having been told the hour and nothing else.
events.arc: A Lesser God Courting Above Their Station

effects.log: A silence. Then a very old elder says, 'Then the house must grow to fit it,' and the vestibule door opens.

choices.text: Say you will raise {him} first: give {him} a domain

effects.log: The elders confer. A crossroads is not nothing, they concede, when it is the first crossroads of a thousand worlds.
You bow. The vestibule door stays closed. {npc} waits all day, and then goes home without having been called.

events.text: It turns out, as these things do, that the crossroads is the most-prayed corner of the lower worlds. The ushers are learning {npc}'s name. A Lineage of the Root sends a delegation to offer you both tribute, to be seen near the pair.
events.arc: A Lesser God Courting Above Their Station

effects.log: The delegation is delighted to witness it. The ushers sweep a path of petals. {npc} laughs at the extravagance and weeps.

choices.text: Wed quietly at the crossroads shrine

mem.note: wed me at my own shrine

effects.log: You wed on the dust of the shrine, with a pilgrim as witness. It is the smallest wedding of the age, and the best.

events.text: The elders grant {npc} a small seat of domain at last: the crossroads, formally named in the Book of Fates, with a stair of its own. {npc} accepts it solemnly. Then {he} comes to you and asks, in a very small voice, if now you might ask {him} properly.
events.arc: A Lesser God Courting Above Their Station

mem.note: asked me properly after my seat

effects.log: You ask, in the vestibule, in front of the elders. {npc} says yes before the sentence is finished.

choices.text: Say you never needed a seat to ask

mem.note: said you never needed my seat

effects.log: 'I know,' {npc} says. 'That is why I wanted one.' The vestibule fills with the smell of road dust and rain.

events.text: A page of the Book of Fates turns by itself, and a herald reads it out in the Court: you are to be wed to {npc}, a god you have met twice, on the date written. The Book does not ask. It is very confident. {npc} has not been asked either.
events.arc: The Consort the Book of Fates Chose

effects.log: 'I will choose my own thread,' you say. The Book rustles, offended. {npc} stares, and then, slowly, applauds.
The herald rolls the page back up. The Book keeps the date open, ominously.

choices.text: Accept the Book without a word

effects.log: You bow to the page. The Court moves on. {npc} watches you the whole of the afternoon, trying to read your face.

events.text: The Book of Fates does not enjoy being refused. A string of small misfortunes finds you over the following year: a missed festival, a spilled cup, a stairway that is one step too many. {npc}, to your surprise, appears at each, tidying, saying nothing.
events.arc: The Consort the Book of Fates Chose

effects.log: {npc} says it is not help. It is spite, on your behalf, against a book {he} has never liked either.

choices.text: Suspect {him} of working for the Book

effects.log: {npc} says it is a fair suspicion, and walks away, and then comes back, and says it still is not true.

choices.text: Ignore the misfortunes and soldier on

effects.log: Soldiering on is a kind of cultivation. You grow stronger, if not luckier.

events.text: A scribe of the Court confides, in the archive at night, that the Book's choosing is no oracle. It is a ledger of what the powers of heaven want: the Book chose you for {npc} because both your Lineages sit on a harvest of faith that the Court means to share.
events.arc: The Consort the Book of Fates Chose

mem.note: told me what the Book is

effects.log: {npc} takes it in silence, then breaks into a long laugh. 'A ledger,' {he} says. 'It is only a ledger. Of course it is.'

choices.text: Keep the secret and use it

mem.note: kept the secret and used it

effects.log: You use it quietly against two rival Lineages. It works. {npc} learns of the source months later.
You burn it. The truth remains; the scribe will say it again to someone braver.

events.text: You and {npc} go together to the lower vault of the Book, uninvited, and stand in front of the page that names you both. The page, faintly, is warm. It waits to see if you have come to mend it, or burn it, or to sign.
events.arc: The Consort the Book of Fates Chose

choices.text: Sign it, of your own free will

mem.note: signed the Book freely beside me

effects.log: You sign. {npc} signs. The Book hums, delighted, thinking it won, and you both know better.

choices.text: Strike out the line and write a new one

mem.note: struck out the Book for me

effects.log: The Book writhes. The Court is scandalised. Your names stand in your own hands, and no one dares unwrite them.

choices.text: Leave the page as it is, unsigned

effects.log: You leave the page and each other, and keep the friendship. The Book writes a note in its margin, which neither of you can read.

events.text: Some years after, a scribe of the Court brings you a final copy of the Book's page, with the date of your union written differently from the first: no longer a command, but a report. {npc} looks it over and says only, 'Better.'
events.arc: The Consort the Book of Fates Chose

effects.log: It hangs in your hall for the next age, with a small sign: The Book Learns.
You burn it with {npc} and watch the ash fall on the Court's steps. The Book makes no further comment.

events.text: Among the prayers rising to your altar there is one that is not a prayer: a small, formal note in a god's hand, tucked in the folds of a farmer's plea for rain. It says only: 'I have been meaning to say good morning.' It is signed {npc}.
events.arc: The Prayer That Was Not a Prayer

effects.log: You tuck 'Good morning' into the next rain you send. It arrives in {npc}'s garden, glittering.

choices.text: Answer with rain, and nothing more

effects.log: {npc} gets only rain. It is a very good rain, and {he} stands out in it for an hour.

choices.text: Pass the note to the Court as a curiosity

effects.log: The Court is charmed. {npc}, a shy god, wishes to be unmade for about a century.

events.text: Every season there is another note hidden in a mortal prayer: a line of a poem, a question about your favourite wind, a pressed leaf. You begin to look forward to the prayers more than the Court. You do not tell anyone why.
events.arc: The Prayer That Was Not a Prayer

choices.text: Hide a reply in a blessing

mem.note: hid a reply in a blessing

effects.log: You tuck a line of your own verse into a harvest blessing. It is read aloud in a village, which is wonderful and terrifying.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to meet, in the open

mem.note: asked to meet in the open

effects.log: 'I would like that,' {npc} writes, 'very much, and I am afraid.' You pick a time anyway.

choices.text: Keep the notes in a box and say nothing

effects.log: The box fills. It is a fine thing to have, and a sad thing to keep.

events.text: The meeting at last, in the Court's gardens, is clumsy and wonderful. {npc} has brought your favourite wind in a jar, and it is the wrong one. You have brought a pressed leaf, and it is the wrong leaf. You are both relieved to be this foolish.
events.arc: The Prayer That Was Not a Prayer

choices.text: Laugh and trade the wrong gifts

effects.log: You trade them, and keep them, and they become the right gifts by the force of the afternoon. You are wed within the decade.

choices.text: Open the wrong wind and let it play

effects.log: The wrong wind is delightful anyway. It plays through the gardens for a year, and the Court calls it the Love Wind.

events.text: A season of notes later, you reply to a prayer from a god of the sea that is also a quiet declaration. You send it to {npc} by way of a mortal fisherman, who delivers it, perplexed. The note is a single word: 'Yes.'
events.arc: The Prayer That Was Not a Prayer

choices.text: Wed by letter, across the Court

effects.log: The marriage is entered in the Book of Fates by correspondence. It is the most formal and least formal union of the age.

choices.text: Walk to {npc}'s door and give the word in person

effects.log: You knock. {npc} opens. You say the word aloud. {He} says it back before you are quite finished.

events.text: The Court's great banquet is masked tonight, by an old custom: no god may name their lineage or their domain, and none may be asked to. {npc}, in a mask of black glass, asks you to dance. You can read nothing about {him} but the way {he} moves.

mem.note: danced in a mask with me

effects.log: You dance three figures. {npc} is a good partner, quiet and exact, with the faintest smell of rain.

ok.log: 'Rain,' you say. {npc} goes still, then nods. 'No one has guessed that in an age,' {he} says.

fail.log: You guess wrong, twice. {npc} says it is rude to guess at a masked ball and dances you into the garden.

effects.log: You decline. {npc} bows and finds another partner. You spend the evening wondering about the rain-smell.

events.text: A year later a note arrives, written on black glass: 'The next ball is masked again. Wear the same mask.' You wear it. {npc} wears the black glass. Neither of you says a word until the third figure, when the same smell of rain arrives.

choices.text: Say your name under the mask

mem.note: told me your name in a mask

effects.log: You say it, quietly. A pause. {npc} says {his} own, and the masks are suddenly very thin.
You keep them. It is its own kind of courtship, wordless and exact, and not unpleasant.

choices.text: Take off the mask in the corridor

effects.log: You do. The corridor is empty. {npc} has not followed; the black glass stays on the dance floor.

mem.note: took off the mask too early

events.text: The last masked ball of the age. {npc} meets you at the door without a mask. {He} is a lesser rain-god of a hill pantheon, plain, and trembling a little. 'I wanted you to see me,' {he} says, 'before you decide.' It is the bravest thing you have seen all age.

effects.log: You take them. They are rain-cold and then warm. The ball falls silent, and then the Court applauds.

choices.text: Take off your own mask too

effects.log: You do, and {npc} nods slowly. The rest of the ball is only the two of you, unmasked, in a far corner.

events.text: Another ball, another mask. {npc} wears the black glass again and you wear yours, and you dance in perfect silence. At the end {npc} bows, and you bow, and neither of you asks a name. It has become the ritual, and nothing else is required.

effects.log: Every age, one night, you meet. It is the most constant thing in your life, and the most unspoken.
'Finally,' {npc} says, and takes off the black glass. The face beneath is as familiar as the smell of rain.

events.text: Long ago you did {npc} a favour: you held back a morning for a god who was late to a dawn. {He} has kept account of it ever since, as gods do. Now {he} arrives at your door and says, stiffly, that {he} has come to pay the debt, in full.

choices.text: Ask what the debt is worth

mem.note: asked what my debt was worth

effects.log: 'One dawn,' {npc} says. 'I have tried to offer a dawn back, but I do not have one. I have been practising an alternative.'

choices.text: Say it was nothing, and refuse payment

effects.log: {npc} is stricken. 'It was not nothing to me,' {he} says. 'A debt unpaid is a stone in the heart.'

choices.text: Take the payment, whatever it is

effects.log: {npc} hands you a small clay jar. It is full of the smell of a morning. You carry it for ages.

events.text: {npc} proposes, in the manner of a contract, to pay the debt by courting you for a year: not, {he} stresses, as a sentiment, but as a settlement. {He} has written a schedule. It includes a picnic.

effects.log: You tick the picnic off in the margin. {npc} forgets to mention the debt on the day, and so do you.

choices.text: Amend it: no picnics, more mornings

effects.log: {npc} amends it with great ceremony. By the end of the year every morning is spent together.

choices.text: Decline the settlement and keep the debt open

effects.log: You keep the debt open. {npc} is irritated, and then, strangely, relieved.

events.text: At the end of the year {npc} lays the schedule on the table, every line ticked, and says in a flat voice that the debt is paid. {He} looks at the paper rather than at you. 'I find I do not want it to be,' {he} says. 'I can think of no clause for that.'

choices.text: Write a new clause: a lifetime

mem.note: wrote a new clause for me

effects.log: You write it in the margin in your own hand. {npc} reads it three times and signs. The picnic basket gets a place of honour.

choices.text: Say you will always owe each other, then

mem.note: said we will always owe each other

effects.log: 'A debt that is never paid,' {npc} says. 'That is the best kind.' It is, in the Court's tongue, a vow.
You tear it up with a small ceremony. The debt is paid, and the ending is a quiet one.

events.text: A mortal of the lower worlds has risen to godhood this age, by a miracle the Court is still arguing about, and been seated among the new gods. {npc} stands at the edge of the hall, unsure where to put {his} hands, and the high Lineages circle with marriage in their eyes.
events.arc: The Mortal Who Became a God

choices.text: Take {him} to the quiet terrace first

mem.note: took me to the quiet terrace

effects.log: On the terrace {npc} sits down and cries a little, because the hall is so large. You say nothing, and pass a cup.

mem.note: introduced me to the best Lineages

effects.log: Five Lineages make offers by dinner. {npc} thanks you politely and is quite pale.
You watch the Lineages bear down. You do not move. {npc} sees you not moving, which is a sort of message.

events.text: {npc} tells you over a long evening about the village {he} came from, a small mill on a river, and the mortals {he} left. {He} had not meant to rise; it was an answered prayer that had gone wrong. {He} is not sure {he} is a god at all.
events.arc: The Mortal Who Became a God

choices.text: Tell {him} gods are mostly such answered mistakes

effects.log: 'Mostly,' you say. {npc} stares, and then laughs so hard that the lamps tremble. It is the first laugh since {he} rose.

choices.text: Offer to help {him} learn the Court

mem.note: offered to teach me the Court

effects.log: You spend a season teaching {him} the forms, the bows, the tangle of precedence. {npc} is quick, and very polite.
You listen all night. It seems to be what {he} needed most.

events.text: The Lineages sense a weakness and press: one of the great houses publishes a claim that {npc}'s rise was irregular and should be struck from the Book. {npc} reads it in the vestibule, and the colour drains from {his} face.
events.arc: The Mortal Who Became a God

mem.note: stood beside me at the hearing

effects.log: You stand at {his} shoulder through the whole hearing. The claim is thrown out, and a few Lineages remember who stood where.
You trade a favour to a god of the Root, and the claim is withdrawn. {npc} knows the price and says nothing.
You stay out. The claim lingers. {npc} hears of your absence and stops visiting the terrace.

events.text: A few years on, {npc} stands in the hall as an equal. Someone has seen to it that the mill by the river has a god-shrine now, in {his} name. {He} cannot stop looking at the prayer-slips from home. 'I would like to go and see,' {he} says. 'Come with me.'
events.arc: The Mortal Who Became a God

choices.text: Go, and wed at the mill

mem.note: wed me at my old mill

effects.log: You wed on the bank of the mill-stream, with mortals watching from the reeds, who think it is a festival. It is.

choices.text: Go, and keep it a journey

effects.log: You walk the village together as strangers. The old miller does not recognise {him}, and tells {him} all the gossip.

events.text: {npc} thrives. A year or two later you find them both, {npc} and the Court, comfortable in the same room. The settlement stands. You and {npc} are friends, in the careful way of those who nearly were more, and the Lineages leave you both alone.
events.arc: The Mortal Who Became a God

effects.log: You stay friends, a long game of cups and Court gossip on a quiet terrace. It is warm, and it is enough.

mem.note: let it fade after the settlement

effects.log: You see each other less. Gods have a long time to forget a close friendship. This one fades gently.

events.text: A village far below has built one small shrine for two gods, for want of the money to build two, and the Court has just noticed: you, and {npc}, a god of a neighbouring domain, are both the object of its prayers. Neither of you was asked.

effects.log: You descend in disguise, side by side. The shrine is small, shabby, and loved. {npc} adjusts a candle without thinking.
You write. {npc} writes back within the hour: 'I am already there. Come.'

choices.text: Leave it to the Court to sort

effects.log: The Court sorts it badly. You hear the village sighing in its prayers for a decade.

events.text: At the shrine a villager prays to both of you in one breath, a little muddled, asking for a good harvest and a good husband. {npc} and you exchange a look across the altar. It is not clear which of you is meant to answer which.

choices.text: Answer the harvest yourself and leave the husband to {him}

effects.log: {npc} laughs aloud, startling a hen. The prayer is split the way it was probably meant to be.
A gentle rain and a stranger on the road. Both answered, together, in a way neither of you planned.

choices.text: Stay silent and let the villager sort it

effects.log: The villager sorts it. The harvest is good, the husband is a cousin, and the village approves.

events.text: The village council, thrilled by the attention, proposes to rebuild the shrine to be larger, on condition that one of you is named patron god and the other lesser. {npc} looks at the plans, then at you. The village waits with hats off.

mem.note: took the lesser place for me

effects.log: You take it, smiling. The council is astonished. {npc} is quiet for a long minute, then takes your hand under the altar cloth.

choices.text: Propose that the shrine have no patron at all

effects.log: The council argues. At last it carves two doors on one front. 'Two doors,' says {npc}, with delight. 'We both fit.'
The shrine stays small and crooked. The village is disappointed and nonetheless faithful.

events.text: A year on, the shrine stands bright with two doors, and {npc} has taken to sleeping in the little back room on the nights of the full moon, to hear the village sing. You find yourself doing the same. There is a second pillow.

effects.log: You wed in the shrine of two doors, with the village in its best clothes. The prayers that night are almost too loud to bear.

choices.text: Keep two doors, two homes, one shrine

effects.log: You keep your own homes and a shared altar. The village accepts the arrangement, calling it the Two-Door Blessing.

events.text: The shrine, small and shabby, does well in the memory of the village. {npc} and you remain on the best of terms: two gods who looked after a quiet corner of the world together for a while, and left it a bit warmer than they found it.

effects.log: Years later you still receive a prayer from the old shrine every harvest, addressed to both of you in the same hand.
You move on. {npc} does too. The shrine goes on, as shrines do, with faith like the weather.

events.text: An upper seat at the Court's high table has fallen vacant, and three gods are known to be courting it: you, a rival, and {npc}, who has the ear of the Book. {npc} approaches you with a smile that is partly charm and partly arithmetic.
events.arc: A Seat at the High Table

choices.text: Say you will win it fairly

effects.log: {npc} laughs. 'Fair,' {he} says. 'What a lovely word. Let us see how it fares at table.'

choices.text: Offer an alliance against the rival

effects.log: {npc} considers it for a long breath. 'Terms,' {he} says. You are both enjoying yourselves already.
You step back. {npc} is surprised, then amused, and the rival is merely relieved.

events.text: The contest for the seat is a year of dinners, each a test: who can answer a prayer most gracefully, who can reconcile two quarrelling Lineages, who can sit longest in silence. {npc} and you keep meeting at the end of each, a little too pleased.
events.arc: A Seat at the High Table
