ok.log: You win by a hair. {npc} lifts a cup to you across the table and says nothing about the margin.

fail.log: {npc} beats you cleanly and then helps you up from your chair, which is somehow worse and better.

choices.text: Throw a round, to see what {he} does

mem.note: threw a round to test me

effects.log: {npc} sees at once. 'Do not do that,' {he} says, low. 'Never do that.' You do not, again.
You lose, and dine, and enjoy it. The rival wins that round and nobody else minds.

events.text: It comes down to the last dinner, to you and {npc}, with the seat in plain sight at the head of the table. The rest of the Court has gone silent. A god of the Silent Drum holds up a hand and says that whoever yields, may ask the other a favour.
events.arc: A Seat at the High Table

effects.log: You yield. The hall inhales. {npc} takes the seat slowly, and looks at you as though you had made a great gift.
You press, and win, and the seat is yours. {npc} bows with great correctness and does not come to dinner for a season.
The hall explodes in argument. The Silent Drum, after a pause, says there is no law against it.

events.text: After the seat is settled, {npc} comes to you on the high terrace, away from the table, and says the contest was the most honest time of {his} life. 'I want to be honest the rest of it with someone,' {he} says. 'Is it you?'
events.arc: A Seat at the High Table

mem.note: asked and heard yes after the seat

effects.log: You say yes. The terrace lamps, which have been bored for an age, light up one by one.

choices.text: Say let us be friends first

effects.log: 'Friends first,' {npc} says, smiling. 'We never did that. It is a good idea.'

events.text: The seat is yours, and {npc} sits beside you at every dinner, polite and watchful, a rival gone cold. The Court has noted it. They whisper that you have won everything and lost the one dinner companion worth having.
events.arc: A Seat at the High Table

mem.note: was invited to a quiet dinner

effects.log: You invite {him} to a quiet dinner away from the High Table. {npc} comes, stiffly, and stays long.

choices.text: Keep the distance, as the seat requires

mem.note: kept the distance after the seat

effects.log: You keep the distance. The seat is cold. The Court is satisfied with its prediction.

events.text: In an age past, Unmyeong's Thread bound you to {npc}, and you cut it, for reasons that seemed right then. Now {npc} is the new keeper of a small altar near yours, and the Thread, faint, spliced by a scribe, has returned to your wrist.

effects.log: {npc} is polite, tired and wary. 'You came,' {he} says. 'I did not expect you to come.'
The Thread parts with a small sad sound. You tell yourself it was kind. {npc} hears the sound from across the Court.
You wait. The Thread does not tighten, but it does not fray either.

events.text: {npc} tells you why the cut hurt: not the cut itself, but the silence after, the age of it. You listen. There is no good answer, and you do not pretend there is. The Thread on your wrist is warmer than you expected.

effects.log: You apologise without a reason attached. {npc} looks at you for a long time, and nods once.
You explain. They were good reasons. {npc} agrees that they were, and says that is the worst part.
You stay. It is not an answer. It is not a refusal either, and {npc} takes it as the first small thing.

events.text: A scribe of the Court mends the Thread properly, with a knot, and says it cannot be cut again by the same hand. {npc} holds the other end of it. There is a shared silence while you both consider what that means.

effects.log: You accept it. The knot holds. {npc} laughs shakily and says it feels like a rope, and that is fine.

choices.text: Ask for the Thread to stay loose

mem.note: asked for the Thread to stay loose

effects.log: The scribe sighs and loosens it. 'A loose thread is still a thread,' {npc} says, and takes up the end like a leash of thin gold.

events.text: You say your reasons again, this time to the end, and they do not improve. {npc} thanks you for the honesty, and for the years. The Thread between you is faint and frayed. You both understand, by the end of the conversation, that it is not going to mend.

effects.log: You become friends, careful and affectionate, with the Thread a ghost on your wrist for an age.
You part. The Thread dissolves into small bright motes. {npc} walks into the Court's evening without looking back.

events.text: Your domain is the weather of a broad valley, and {npc}'s is its harvest, and the two of you have just discovered that this is not the same thing. You send rain on the third day for the young wheat. {npc} sends the sun the same morning for the barley. The valley gets a mudslide.

mem.note: proposed a schedule after the mudslide

effects.log: {npc} agrees with relief. By evening you have a chart on the wall: rain at night, sun by day, with sulks on Thursdays.
{npc} says the wheat was not the point and the barley was, and the argument goes on until the mud has dried on the whole valley.

choices.text: Ask the valley what it wants

effects.log: A village headwoman prays a long, confused prayer. It comes down to both, but not at once. You carry it home as a small peace offering.

events.text: The schedule works for a season and then fails at the first drought-year, when there is neither rain nor sun enough to go round. You and {npc} sit at opposite ends of the table with a map of the valley between you, pointing at the same two villages.

effects.log: You give it. {npc} says nothing for a long time, and then, quietly, gives you the second.

choices.text: Take both and promise a better year

effects.log: You take both, and promise. {npc} watches you go, and does not argue, which is worse than arguing.

choices.text: Split the weather and the sun by hour

effects.log: A tight, difficult schedule. The two villages muddle through, and you both grow thin with the effort.

events.text: The valley's harvest festival comes. Both of you are named in the prayers, a hundred times, as the Giver of Rain and the Giver of Grain, which the villagers do not distinguish. A child asks which of you is the stronger. The village goes quiet.

choices.text: Say you are two halves of one gift

effects.log: The village sighs happily. {npc} squeezes your hand under the festival cloth, which is the right size to hide it.
{npc} protests, then blushes, then spends the rest of the festival being very proud and rather silly.
The village cheers. {npc} smiles a moment too long. You are not forgiven until the next harvest.

events.text: A blight comes to the valley's wheat, and neither rain nor sun will cure it. It needs both at once, held in a single narrow hour. The two domains, joined, could do it. The villagers pray. {npc} stands at the field's edge and holds out a hand.

choices.text: Join domains and cure the blight

mem.note: joined domains to cure the blight

effects.log: Rain and sun, in one hour. The blight burns away like mist. The valley sings that night, and so does {npc}, off-key.

ok.log: You manage it, barely. {npc} says nothing, and has eyes like old coin.

mem.note: tried the blight alone and failed

fail.log: You fail. The blight spreads. {npc} steps in without a word and mends what can be mended.

events.text: A harvest of the best barley in a hundred years makes you and {npc} the talk of the Court. The Lineage of the Root offers a union of the two domains into one office, with a single seat, a joint name and a very good stipend. {npc} looks at you.

mem.note: took a joint office with me

effects.log: A seat for two. The Court calls you the Valley, and you do not mind the name.
You decline. The Root is irked. {npc} says that is exactly right, and goes to see about the barley.

events.text: You are the god of one border and {npc} the god of its peace, a pairing the Court thought neat until the first skirmish of the age broke out on the border and each of you answered it. Soldiers on both sides are praying to the same couple, for opposite results.
events.arc: The War God and the Peace God

effects.log: You answer the soldiers' prayer for courage. {npc} answers the widows' for mercy. The prayers meet in the middle and do not match.

mem.note: answered for the widows with me

effects.log: You and {npc} sit up all night together over the border's prayers. By dawn the skirmish is over.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch the border

effects.log: You watch. Neither domain moves. The skirmish ends in exhaustion, and no one thanks either of you.

events.text: A herald of the Silent Drum asks for a ruling: which of the two of you has authority at the border? {npc} looks at you across the Court's floor. It is an old law, and an old rivalry, and both of you had hoped never to see it invoked.
events.arc: The War God and the Peace God

effects.log: The herald records it. The Drum shrugs, a thunder far away. {npc} takes the authority as one takes a fragile thing.
You claim it. The Drum is satisfied. {npc} bows, and the frost in the bow lasts a year.

choices.text: Ask for the ruling to be a joint one

effects.log: The Drum has never granted one. It does now, with a long, sullen rumble.

events.text: A winter comes in which war is cheap and peace is dear. The border villages pray for both, in alternating verses. {npc} finds you at the edge of the Court at night, looking down, and says: 'We could do what they ask. Both. Alternately.'
events.arc: The War God and the Peace God

mem.note: tried the alternating verses with me

effects.log: You answer one verse, {npc} the next. It is the ugliest working you have ever done, and it holds the border all winter.

choices.text: Refuse: a border cannot be both

mem.note: said a border cannot be both

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. 'Then one of us loses,' {he} says. Neither of you wants to be the one to say which.

events.text: The border settles. The villages, through the winter, learned to pray to both of you in the same breath, in a new prayer that is half a battle-cry and half a lullaby. The Court is baffled by it. You and {npc} sing it to each other, softly, at night.
events.arc: The War God and the Peace God

mem.note: sang the border prayer with me

effects.log: You sing it, in harmony. It does not scan. It works. The border is quiet for the rest of the age.

mem.note: taught the Court our border prayer

effects.log: You teach it. The Court takes it up grumbling. Soon a dozen borders are singing it, and the Drum rumbles approval.

events.text: You are a god of the day's last light, and {npc} of the night's first dark: you meet only at dusk, for the length of a breath, at the exact edge of both your domains. Every day. The Court finds this romantic. You find it a very short conversation.

choices.text: Use the breath well: a single sentence

mem.note: gave me one sentence a day

effects.log: You have your sentence prepared each dusk. It is a good game, and some days you say a very good one.

choices.text: Ask the Court to lengthen the dusk

effects.log: The Court agrees to a few extra heartbeats in each dusk. It is more than anyone before has asked for, and {npc} is touched.

choices.text: Write each other letters in the daylight and dark

effects.log: A letter left on the horizon each day, answered by the next. It is slow, and each line is considered.

events.text: A solar eclipse, an hour long, a gap in the Court's calendar: the day and the night overlap, and for one hour you and {npc} may share a sky. You have both been waiting for it for centuries. It is hard to remember what you meant to say.

choices.text: Spend it in silence, just together

mem.note: spent the eclipse in silence with me

effects.log: An hour of grey light, a hand in a hand, nobody speaking. {npc} cries a little, and you do not mention it.

choices.text: Talk the whole hour, a hundred centuries of things

effects.log: You talk until the sun is back. {npc} says it was not enough, and also that it was more than enough.
You are very tired, and fall asleep with {npc} beside you. You wake to a quiet, ordinary dusk and the rueful look of {him}.

events.text: A comet, a lesser god, or a plain mistake has put a dawn into the middle of your night, and the Court has asked you both to sort it. {npc} is annoyed. You are charmed. The dawn is brighter than yours, and rather rude.

mem.note: dimmed the stray dawn with me

effects.log: You dim it together, light and dark meeting. It is the longest conversation you two have had in an age.

choices.text: Leave it, and watch it from the same hill

mem.note: watched the stray dawn with me

effects.log: You watch it from a hill you share for the one night. The Court complains. You do not hear.

events.text: The Court at last redraws the borders of the hours. The dusk is lengthened to a quarter of a day, by common consent, on the grounds that you two are the only ones in the Court who are still in love. You and {npc} sit through the long dusk and say nothing.

mem.note: thanked the Court for our dusk

effects.log: The Court shrugs and bows. A quarter of a day is a lot of time to share. You and {npc} make good use of it.

choices.text: Say it was never about the hours

mem.note: said it was never the hours

effects.log: 'The hours were a game,' you say. {npc} nods. The long dusk goes on, and so does everything else.

events.text: {npc} is the god of a mountain; you are the sea at its feet. Marriage has put your domains in constant touch, which is lovely until the spring floods come, and the mountain's melt meets your tide on the coast, and a fishing village drowns its roofs.

choices.text: Turn your tide back at once

mem.note: turned back the tide for me

effects.log: You turn the tide. The village is spared a worse flood, and your waters have never felt so strained.

mem.note: asked me to slow the melt

effects.log: {npc} slows it. The mountain groans, and the village is saved, and you both feel like you did something rather difficult.

choices.text: Do nothing, and let the valley decide

effects.log: The valley decides to flood. The village rebuilds on the hill, which is wiser, and nobody thanks either of you.

events.text: The fishing village has rebuilt, and its people pray to both of you now, fearfully: sea, mountain, spare us. They have carved a figure of each on the new pier. {npc} is vexed that yours is larger. You are vexed that {his} is better made.

mem.note: had a better figure of me carved

effects.log: The carvers outdo themselves. {npc} comes down to see it, goes quiet, and kisses the stone cheek.
A small pebble of a chip, a great pleasure. {npc} laughs at you for a month.

choices.text: Leave both figures as they are

effects.log: The figures stand side by side on the pier, unequal, in the salt wind. The village loves them.

events.text: A storm is coming up the coast, a great one, with the sea beneath it and the mountain in its way. The two of you could meet it as one: a sea-wall of water, a stone shoulder of land. It would cost you both dearly in qi, in grace, in the worlds' faith.

mem.note: stood against the storm with me

effects.log: The sea rises as a wall and the mountain leans as a shoulder. The storm breaks on you both. The coast, behind, sleeps.

choices.text: Steer the storm out to sea alone

ok.log: You push it out to open water. It takes a great deal, and {npc} watches the whole thing from the mountaintop, a little hurt not to have been asked.

mem.note: tried the storm alone and was hurt

fail.log: The storm is bigger than you thought. {npc} comes down the mountain in a rage and hauls you out of the surf.

events.text: After the storm the coast has a new shape: a long bay sheltered by an arm of the mountain, where the sea now lies still. Ships bless the bay by both your names. {npc} sits beside you on the new headland, and says it is the best view in any world.

mem.note: agreed the bay was the best view

effects.log: You sit till the stars rise in the bay, doubled in water. You do not feel like leaving.
The bay is named in the Book of Fates before the week is out. {npc} says nothing, and the mountain, at its back, quakes happily.

events.text: You are a weaver of fate, close to Unmyeong's own work, and {npc} is a god of chance, whose whole domain is the thing you are trying to prevent. At your table {he} sits happily on a thread you spent a week untangling, and asks what it was for.

effects.log: {npc} listens, enchanted. 'So that is why the coin always lands that way,' {he} says. 'I had wondered.'
{npc} laughs, falls, and lands on another thread. Five more have to be untangled by sundown.
'For the things not worth planning,' {npc} says. 'Which is most things.' You write that down in the margin of your loom.

events.text: A prophecy in your loom, long laid, is about to fall due, and {npc} has found it and stepped on the knot. The result is a wild, unplanned improvement: a young god set to die will live, and a minor war will be skipped. You are furious, and wondering.

choices.text: Mend the knot and restore the plan

mem.note: mended the knot against my luck

effects.log: You mend it. The young god dies as planned, and the war goes ahead. {npc} says nothing for a week.

choices.text: Leave the improvement and learn from it

effects.log: You leave it. The young god lives and writes you a thank-you note, which you pin to your loom.
A moth carries the question up. It comes back with a single word: 'Both.'

events.text: The Court has been warned by Unmyeong's moth that fate and fortune are drifting apart and may soon unpick a thousand years of order. It wants you and {npc} to explain yourselves. You stand before it, hand in hand, and the Court asks which of you is the stronger.

choices.text: Say fate is, and fortune is the proof

effects.log: The Court nods. {npc} does not contradict you in public, and does so thoroughly at home.

choices.text: Say they are the same thread, seen from two sides

mem.note: said we were the same thread

effects.log: The Court argues. Unmyeong's moth lands on your joined hands and does not move for an hour.

choices.text: Say it is not for the Court to decide

effects.log: A scandal. The Court takes it badly and the younger gods applaud.

events.text: Your loom and {npc}'s coin are placed together by the Court on a single table in the hall, as a symbol. A small mortal child, brought up to see the gods, tugs a thread and rolls the coin at once. Nothing happens. Both of you laugh until you cry.

choices.text: Keep the table as it is

effects.log: The table stays, and so do you. Mortal children are brought to tug the thread and roll the coin, and nothing ever happens.

choices.text: Weave the coin into a thread

mem.note: wove the coin into a thread

effects.log: A single bright thread, with a coin in it. It becomes the Court's seal for the age.

events.text: Years after the wedding the two of your domains begin to overlap in a way no one planned: a small patch of the world below where both are present, and which answers to neither. A third thing is growing there, like a seed in two palms.
events.arc: The Domain Neither of You Owned

mem.note: tended the new domain with me

effects.log: You and {npc} water it with grace. It grows a shoot, then a bud, then a small bewildered flower.
The Court sends a surveyor. {npc} is not pleased, but understands. The flower is measured and filed.
You watch it grow. It is a very small thing, and you find you are afraid of it.

events.text: The new domain is a kind of kindness: the small glad habit of a household, the warmth between two people who have stopped arguing. Mortals in the area begin to pray to it, though it has no name. {npc} suggests, shyly, that you name it.
events.arc: The Domain Neither of You Owned

choices.text: Name it for the two of you

effects.log: You name it with a syllable from each of your names. The Book of Fates accepts it, bemused.
You leave it. The mortals call it The Warm, and that name, in the end, is the one that sticks.
They name it badly and with feeling. {npc} laughs for an hour.

events.text: A rival Lineage claims the new domain. They say it arose in their sphere, from theirs, and demand its tithes. {npc} and you stand at the Court, a pair holding a flower, facing a delegation holding a ledger.
events.arc: The Domain Neither of You Owned

effects.log: You cite the Book of Fates in six places. The delegation withdraws. The flower is yours, by the paper.

choices.text: Defend it with a show of joined power

ok.log: You and {npc} unleash your united domains for a breath. The delegation sits down very suddenly.

mem.note: defended the domain with me, barely

fail.log: The joined power is clumsy. You lose face. The flower survives, mostly.

effects.log: The rival is dumbfounded. A share is agreed, small, and the claim lapses.

events.text: The new domain is accepted into the Book of Fates at last, and the Court gives you both the title of Keepers. {npc} cries a little in the Court, and you hold {his} elbow, and the flower stands in a small jar on a plinth, absurd and perfect.
events.arc: The Domain Neither of You Owned

effects.log: You accept. The jar is polished daily. The domain thrives in the world below, small and warm.

choices.text: Refuse the title, keep the work

mem.note: refused the title and kept the work

effects.log: You refuse the title with a bow. {npc} follows, and the Court mutters that it is the most modest couple of the age.

events.text: Another delegation, another ledger: the rival has gone to the Court on a technicality, and the new domain is, for the moment, disputed. {npc} makes tea. You fill in forms. Neither of you can bring yourself to hate the rival entirely.
events.arc: The Domain Neither of You Owned

choices.text: Fill in the forms with care

effects.log: You fill them in with great care, in double columns. The dispute is resolved by the end of the century.

choices.text: Brew tea and wait it out

mem.note: brewed tea and waited with me

effects.log: You wait. It takes eighty years. Tea is brewed throughout. You are both very well hydrated.

events.text: An old shepherd in a hill village prays to {npc} for a good lambing, by name, and prays at length. It is your domain. {npc} reads the prayer and goes quiet. 'What do we do?' {he} asks. 'It is yours. The prayer used my name.'

choices.text: Answer it yourself and pass the credit

effects.log: You answer it, and send a dream that gives {npc} the thanks. The lambing is excellent, and the grandmother thinks {npc} a marvel.
You whisper the right pass of the blessing to {npc}, who delivers it with great dignity. The lambs are lovely.

choices.text: Correct the shepherd in a dream

effects.log: You tell the shepherd gently who was meant. They wake unconvinced, and keeps praying to {npc}, who is delighted.

events.text: The error spreads. The whole village prays to {npc} for lambs, and to you for fishing, both of which are the wrong way round. The two of you have started to answer each other's prayers, in secret. A priest at the shrine has noticed.

choices.text: Swap domains for a season, openly

effects.log: You swap. The village is dumbfounded. The lambs are fine. The fishing is, if anything, better than before.

choices.text: Appear in a dream to the priest and explain

effects.log: The priest wakes in tears and changes the shrine's plaque. The village adjusts, a little confused.
You keep answering. The village is satisfied, and the Court, which has noticed, files a note.

events.text: A rival god of a neighbouring village, hearing of the confusion, starts to answer the prayers in person, taking credit for both. The villagers are impressed. {npc} is incensed on your behalf. You are incensed on {his}.

effects.log: You and {npc} walk in on the rival at dawn. The rival is polite, panicked, and gives the credit back with a bow.

choices.text: Let the rival have the credit

effects.log: You let the rival. The village loves the rival for a century, and then forgets. You and {npc} laugh at the memory.
You answer louder. It is vulgar and effective. The village returns to its original gods.

events.text: The village builds a new shrine, to both of you, on the hill where the shepherd prayed. The shepherd comes to the opening with a basket of lamb-bread. She prays, aloud, to the two of you at once, correctly this time. She winks, up at the sky, as if she had known.

effects.log: The lambs come twice as numerous that spring. The shepherd says, to nobody, that they knew it all along.

choices.text: Come down in disguise and eat the bread

mem.note: ate lamb-bread with me in disguise

effects.log: You and {npc} descend in plain cloaks and eat the lamb-bread on the hill. It is delicious.

events.text: The faithful of the lower worlds have raised a temple to you both, and the plans have arrived for approval: one altar, one roof, two sets of offerings. {npc} studies the drawings and points out, mildly, that your side has the better window.

effects.log: You swap. The window is as good as promised. {npc} is moved enough to hang a lantern in it every evening.
You argue for it. {npc} gives way, in the end, and the window is yours, and the pleasure is a little sour.
The plans are approved. The window, you note, is on neither side, but in the middle, which is a relief.

events.text: The temple opens. The first week brings a flood of pilgrims, and the offerings are split in the old way: grain to one, incense to the other. But the priests, who have never run a temple for two, begin to count the candles on each side.

effects.log: You count, and you find that the two sides are exactly even, which is a sort of miracle.

choices.text: Tell the priests not to count

mem.note: told the priests not to count

effects.log: The priests are relieved, and slightly shocked. The count stops. The temple grows warmer.
You quietly prefer your own. The priests learn which side to light first. {npc} learns too.

events.text: A schism: half the pilgrims pray only to you, half only to {npc}, and the temple's single roof now covers two congregations that will not share a bench. The priests ask the two of you to say something to the faithful, together.

choices.text: Appear in a single dream, hand in hand

mem.note: appeared in a dream, hand in hand

effects.log: You appear to the whole temple in one dream: two hands in one. The congregations wake in tears and share a bench.
The priests settle it, with a rota. It works well enough, in a dry sort of way.

events.text: A century on, the temple is a place of pilgrimage for the newly wed. They kneel at your double altar and ask for the blessing of both. {npc} and you watch, from the cloud above, some of the couples you have helped become ancient, then dust.

choices.text: Bless the next couple in person

mem.note: blessed the next couple beside me

effects.log: You and {npc} descend, unseen, and bless them with a hand each on their joined hands. They never know, and are always lucky.
You watch, and talk about every one. It becomes your favourite pastime, and theirs.

events.text: The temple's rota has a hundred rules now. A new head priest wants to simplify it, by dropping one of you from the altar on weekdays. It is an administrative convenience. {npc} reads the letter aloud, in a flat voice, and looks up.

mem.note: refused to be dropped from the altar

effects.log: You refuse. The head priest backs down, fumbling. The rota stays complicated and the altar stays double.

mem.note: agreed to be dropped on weekdays

effects.log: You agree, on condition that you are each dropped on opposite days. The head priest has to think about that for a decade.

events.text: It starts with a small quarrel over a thread of the loom, the kind that ends before supper. This time it does not. {npc} goes to the far terrace and says nothing, and you say nothing, and by the end of the week the silence has acquired furniture.

effects.log: You go to the far terrace and say it. {npc} nods, and the silence cracks along one seam, though it does not break.
You wait. The silence grows a second chair. A year goes by. Then a decade.
You throw yourself into the loom. Thread after thread, until the house is full of very fine cloth and no conversation.

events.text: A decade of silence. The Court finds it funny, in the way gods find the small domestic wars of others funny, and sends a mutual friend with a plate of honey-cakes. {npc} and you eat in different rooms and compare notes by the crumbs.

choices.text: Send a crumb back with a note

mem.note: sent a note back with a crumb

effects.log: The note says only: Good cakes. The crumb comes back with the reply: They were.

choices.text: Thank the friend and say nothing

mem.note: thanked the friend and said nothing

effects.log: The friend leaves puzzled. The honey-cakes go stale in two rooms.
The friend says: 'Nothing, loudly.' You laugh, and then, alone, you do not.

events.text: A half-century. The silence has become a kind of language, with its own grammar of doors closing and cups set down. You find, to your surprise, that you can tell {npc}'s mood from the sound of {his} footsteps across the Court at night.

effects.log: You walk in time with {him} across the Court one night. {npc} does not look round. {His} pace slows to yours.

choices.text: Leave the door open at night

effects.log: You leave your door open a hand's width. In the morning there is a cup of tea on the sill, steaming.
You pretend. {npc} notices you pretending, and is oddly touched.

events.text: The seventieth year. The Court's scribes record the silence as the longest marital silence of the age. A cheerful young god asks the two of you for the secret. {npc} and you look at each other, across a hall, for the first time in decades.

choices.text: Say it was never silence, only listening

effects.log: {npc} lets out a laugh like a cracked bell. The young god writes it down.

choices.text: Say the secret is to speak first, next time

effects.log: A small crowd gathers. {npc} says, quietly, 'I hope so,' and the Court holds its breath.
The young god, deflated, goes away. {npc} makes a sound like the beginning of a joke.

events.text: The century ends not with a quarrel's resolution but with an ordinary morning: {npc} comes into the room, sits down, and says, 'The thread was blue, you know. I was right about the thread.' You have been right about the thread for a hundred years.

choices.text: Say you were never right about the thread

mem.note: conceded the thread after a century

effects.log: You concede. {npc} sits back, delighted, and from that day onward the house is full of noise, endlessly, gladly.

mem.note: argued the thread after a century

effects.log: And you are off again, the two of you, arguing the thread. It is the first conversation in a century and it lasts three days.

events.text: The silence never ends. The years pile up. You and {npc} become a fixture of the Court, the pair that does not speak, and gods make small pilgrimages to the far terraces where you sit. Perhaps it is love, of an unusual shape. Perhaps not.

choices.text: Accept the silence as a shape of love

mem.note: let the silence be a love

effects.log: You accept it. It is not what you wanted, but it is what you have, and it has its own tenderness.

choices.text: Leave the Court for a while

effects.log: You leave. It is time to think. When you return, the silence is waiting, much as you left it.

events.text: A courier from {npc}'s Lineage announces that the elders of the house will visit for an age, to see how their kinsman fares in the new home. You have a week. The courier hands you a list of their preferences, which is eleven scrolls long.

choices.text: Read the list, all eleven scrolls

effects.log: You read them all. They contradict one another in four places. You make a note and begin to prepare, resigned.

choices.text: Throw the list in the fire

effects.log: It burns well. {npc} stares, then, after a pause, laughs in horror and admiration.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to tell you what they actually want

effects.log: 'Tea,' {npc} says. 'And to be asked about the weather. Everything else is performance.' You make a better list.

events.text: The elders arrive on a cloud with a retinue of nineteen servants, and inspect the house in silence while {npc} hovers by the door. The eldest runs a finger over the lintel and shows it to the others. There is nothing on it. They look very disappointed.

choices.text: Serve them tea and ask about the weather

effects.log: The eldest, startled, begins to talk about the weather. By dinner the entire Lineage is sharing opinions about the clouds.

choices.text: Show them the loom or the work of the house

effects.log: They examine your work with exacting care. The eldest says it is 'adequate,' which in the Lineage is a hymn.

choices.text: Apologise for the lack of dust

effects.log: The elders are confused, then amused. The ice breaks a little.

events.text: On the third week the eldest takes you aside, while {npc} is out of earshot, and says that the Lineage is not satisfied: {npc} is unhappy, in the manner of people who do not complain. 'What are you doing wrong?' the eldest asks. It is not rhetorical. They want a list.

choices.text: Say you do not know, and ask for help

effects.log: The eldest is deeply startled. Then, slowly, kindly, they tell you three things, all of them true.

choices.text: Say {npc} is happy and ask to be believed

effects.log: The eldest looks at you for a long time, then at {npc}, who is blushing. 'Hm,' says the eldest.

choices.text: Say it is none of their business

effects.log: The eldest takes this with perfect calm, which is worse. The Lineage packs the next morning.

mem.note: said it was none of their business

events.text: The elders leave at last, in the same cloud, with the same nineteen servants, and a shy note from the eldest: 'The tea was adequate.' {npc} reads it aloud twice. You both know this is the warmest thing the eldest has ever written.

effects.log: It hangs by the door, a little crooked. Visitors are told its importance. They do not understand, and are told again.
You write: 'The tea was adequate also.' The eldest will treasure it for an age.

events.text: Word has reached the lower worlds that two gods are wed and living in the Court, and pilgrims have begun to climb the sky to see it. A line of tiny mortals waits on the cloud stair, holding gifts, staring up at your windows. {npc} peeks through the curtain.

effects.log: You receive them in a rota. They are shy, wide-eyed, and adorable. {npc} is very good at it, and you tell {him} so.

choices.text: Send a dream telling them to go home

mem.note: told the pilgrims to go home

effects.log: They go home, disappointed and relieved. A few pray to the dream.

choices.text: Pretend you are not at home

effects.log: You hide, giggling, behind the curtain with {npc}. The pilgrims leave their gifts at the door.

events.text: One pilgrim, a small child, has climbed the whole stair alone to ask for a parent's cough to be cured. The child stands at the door, shaking. {npc} gets down on one knee to meet the child's eyes, as if it is the most natural thing.

mem.note: cured the pilgrim's mother with me

effects.log: You cure it. The child cries with relief. {npc} sends the child home with honey-cakes and a stern lecture on stairs.

mem.note: walked the pilgrim home with me

effects.log: You descend with the child. The parent is already getting better, which is a blessing you did not need to send.

choices.text: Send the child home with a blessing and no cure

effects.log: The cough remains. The mother prays again next month. You do better the second time.

mem.note: sent the pilgrim away without a cure

events.text: Years later the line on the cloud stair is a legend, and a festival: the Day of the Door, held on the anniversary of the child's climb, when anyone may knock on a god's door once a year. You open the door to find a woman with a cough-remedy herb, laughing.

choices.text: Accept the herb and invite the visitor in

effects.log: This is the child, now grown. You and {npc} give them tea, and the Day of the Door becomes a festival for all the heavens.

mem.note: thanked the pilgrim at the door

effects.log: You thank her warmly, and she goes down the stair again, to a life of her own.

events.text: You and {npc} have been housed by the Court in a cloud pavilion that neither of you chose. It has twelve rooms, a fountain that sings flat, and a view of the Court's laundry. {npc} wants to move. You rather like the fountain.

effects.log: You pick a small cloud on the western rim, with a view of sunsets and no laundry. The fountain comes too, flat as ever.
You redecorate. {npc} chooses the curtains. The fountain is retuned, slightly.

choices.text: Ask the Court for a better pavilion

effects.log: The Court sends a catalogue of eleven pavilions. None is better. {npc} laughs until the page curls.

events.text: The new cloud, or the old one, needs a garden. {npc} wants sky-roses, which grow only on a god's patience. You want something sensible, such as moss. The two of you stand at the garden's edge with a trowel each, and one pot.

effects.log: The sky-roses take an age to bloom and are worth it. {npc} sits by them every evening, humming.
The moss thrives. It is green, restful and dull, and {npc} forgives you in about a decade.
You plant the moss under the roses. They help each other. Neither of you will admit it.

events.text: The house settles into itself over a few ages. One evening you come home to find the lamps lit and the table laid, and {npc} in a chair, grinning. 'Ten ages today,' {he} says. 'I kept count. You didn't.' You didn't.

choices.text: Admit you did not keep count

effects.log: {npc} says that is why {he} kept it for both of you. You eat together under the lamps and lose count of the evening.

choices.text: Say you counted the evenings, not the ages

effects.log: 'Which is more,' {npc} says, after a moment, 'than the ages.' It is a very small, very good answer.

events.text: An age has passed since your union was entered in the Book of Fates, and the Court's heralds have appointed a feast, a reading and an honour for the pair. {npc} is dreading it. You find, to your surprise, that you are looking forward to it.

choices.text: Tell {npc} you are looking forward to it

mem.note: said you were glad of the feast

effects.log: {npc} stares at you. 'Truly?' {he} asks. You are, a little. It spreads, as these things do.
'No,' {npc} says, after a moment. 'We should go. I just wanted to be asked.'
You write it. It is thirty pages. {npc} reads it and weeps and says it must be cut to one.

events.text: At the feast a herald reads a list of the age's marriages, and ends with yours: 'The longest-lived, and the quietest.' A ripple of amusement. {npc} squeezes your hand under the cloth. The honour is a small bronze lamp.

effects.log: You receive it side by side. It burns with a steady, warm light, and the Court applauds, a little uncertainly.

mem.note: made a short speech for us

effects.log: You say six words: 'We are still arguing about the thread.' The hall roars. The lamp is yours.

choices.text: Pass the lamp to a younger couple

effects.log: The younger couple blush and stammer. The Court is touched.

events.text: The lamp burns by your bed for another age, and then another. You and {npc} grow old in a god's way, without growing old at all: only more yourselves. One evening {npc} looks at the lamp and says it is time to light a new one for the next pair.

choices.text: Light a new lamp for strangers

mem.note: lit a new lamp with me

effects.log: You light it and leave it on the Court's step with no name. A young pair finds it that night and takes it home.

mem.note: kept the old lamp with me

effects.log: You keep it. It burns on, and you watch it with {npc}, into the next age and the one after.

events.text: You find {npc} in your hall of offerings at night, reading the ledger of your faith by lamplight, with a pen in hand. {He} does not hide it. 'I was only checking the sums,' {he} says. The sums are in your handwriting, and {he} has corrected two.
events.arc: The Consort Who Wanted Your Domain

mem.note: asked why I checked the sums

effects.log: 'Because someone should,' {npc} says. It is partly true. The correction was right, and you are not sure that you like that.
You thank {him} and shut the book. {npc} looks, for a moment, almost disappointed that you did not mind.

choices.text: Take the ledger and lock it away

effects.log: You take it. {npc} says nothing, in a way that has an edge. The lock is a good one, and the key is on your sleeve.

events.text: Over the following year, small things shift: a prayer to you reaches {npc} first, a rite is done in {his} hand rather than yours, a pilgrim asks politely whose domain it is. {He} is capable, and gentle, and the faithful are adjusting.
events.arc: The Consort Who Wanted Your Domain

effects.log: {npc} says that {he} never meant to take anything. {His} eyes say that {he} meant to be asked.

mem.note: was given a share of the rites

effects.log: You offer {him} a share. {npc} takes it as a gift, and the faithful pray to both. The ledger is a lot easier to read.
You take them all back in a week. The faithful are bewildered. {npc} is cool and perfectly polite for a century.

mem.note: took the rites back all at once

events.text: A herald of the Court arrives with a petition, signed by {npc}, asking that the domain be formally split in two, with {npc} as its second keeper. It is neatly drawn, with good reasons. You find it very hard to be angry, and you are, a little.
events.arc: The Consort Who Wanted Your Domain

effects.log: You sign. {npc} reads the signature three times and then looks up with a face you have not seen since the wedding.

choices.text: Refuse and offer a smaller concession

effects.log: You offer a smaller thing, a shared seat, and {npc} accepts it, evenly, and plans the next move.

choices.text: Take the petition to the Court as an insult

effects.log: The Court takes it as an insult. {npc} is shamed and does not forget it.

mem.note: took our petition as an insult

events.text: The domain is split, and both halves prosper. {npc} is a good keeper, fairer than you in a few things and worse in others, and the faithful, in their shrines below, learn two names where they once knew one. At the end of the age {npc} comes home, tired and very happy.
events.arc: The Consort Who Wanted Your Domain

effects.log: You greet {him} with tea and a stack of notes. {npc} laughs, and sits, and the notes are read late into the night.
You hold out your arms. {npc} walks into them, and says nothing. The split has not changed this.

events.text: The shared seat is a poor compromise. {npc} reads it as an insult and you read it as a gift, and the two of you spend a century sharing a chair in the Court like two cats in one basket. Only at the very end do you find a way to discuss it honestly.
events.arc: The Consort Who Wanted Your Domain

choices.text: Give the full domain at last

effects.log: You give it. {npc} accepts it quietly, and thanks you for the century, and for the cat-basket.

choices.text: Keep the compromise as a game

mem.note: kept the compromise as a game

effects.log: You keep the chair and the argument both. It becomes the permanent shape of your marriage, a long affectionate fight.

events.text: {npc}'s plan is brought to light by a scribe of the Court: a quiet attempt to move the faith of your domain into {his} own over three ages, thread by thread, in a way that would never have been noticed. The scribe puts the evidence in your hands.
events.arc: The Consort Who Wanted Your Domain

effects.log: {npc} reads the evidence, goes white, and says 'I would have told you.' It is not clear {he} would.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch what {he} does next

mem.note: was watched after my plan came out

effects.log: You say nothing. {npc} sees that you know, and the next three months are unbearably gentle.

events.text: {npc} has been asked to sit as a substitute at the Heavenly Court for a single session, and came home glowing. At supper {he} says, carefully, that {he} has been thinking, and that a permanent seat, an actual one, with a cushion, would suit {him}.
events.arc: A Seat in the Heavenly Court

choices.text: Say you will support the petition

mem.note: said you would support my petition

effects.log: You promise your voice at the Court. {npc} lights up like a lamp. The cushion, you gather, has been chosen.

choices.text: Ask what the seat is for

mem.note: asked what the seat was for

effects.log: 'To be heard,' {npc} says, at last. It is simple, and you hear in it a thirst you had not seen.

choices.text: Say the Court is a nest of vipers

effects.log: You say it. {npc} agrees, and goes on wanting the seat, and now has one more reason to think you do not understand.

events.text: The Court demands that a petitioner for a seat show a deed that moved the heavens. {npc} has none. {He} has a hundred small ones: a river steered, a famine ended, a plague soothed. The Court thinks them small. {npc} thinks they are the world.
events.arc: A Seat in the Heavenly Court

choices.text: Help {him} frame them as a single deed

effects.log: You help {him} weave them into one story: The Gentle Years. It is accurate, well told, and the Court begins to listen.

choices.text: Offer one of your own deeds as {his}

mem.note: offered me one of your deeds

effects.log: {npc} refuses, with a proud, hurt face. 'It must be mine,' {he} says. 'Or what is it for?'
{npc} frames them alone, badly, and does not thank you for staying out of it.

events.text: At the hearing a senior god of the Silent Drum asks {npc} if the seat is wanted for the world or for rank. {npc} looks at you in the gallery. The Court hangs on the pause. It is a question with only one honest answer.
events.arc: A Seat in the Heavenly Court

choices.text: Nod to {him}, to tell the truth

effects.log: {npc} says: 'Both. Rank is how the world is heard.' It is a daring answer, and the Court respects it.
{npc} says the polished answer, and gets the vote. {He} is glad, and a little hollow, and does not look at you.
You stand and say what {he} has done. The gallery is moved. The vote is closer than {he} deserves, and it works.

mem.note: spoke for me at my hearing

events.text: The seat is granted. {npc} sits on the cushion at the next session and is, within a decade, one of the most listened-to gods at the Court. It changes {him}. Not for the worse. {He} comes home later now, with more to say, and less to listen to.
events.arc: A Seat in the Heavenly Court

effects.log: You welcome it. {npc} is grateful in a way that goes deeper than words and lasts longer than the cushion.

choices.text: Ask {him} to leave some of the Court at the door

mem.note: asked me to leave the Court at the door

effects.log: {npc} agrees, and means it, and forgets for a while, and you remind {him} again and again.

events.text: The seat is granted by a bare majority, and {npc} understands what the margin means. {He} thanks you for the lie of looking away, in a voice with no thanks in it. The seat is {his}, and it is cold, and the cushion does not warm.
events.arc: A Seat in the Heavenly Court

mem.note: was apologised to for looking away

effects.log: You apologise. {npc} accepts it, slowly, and the cushion grows a little warmer in the following age.

choices.text: Say the vote is the vote

mem.note: was told the vote is the vote

effects.log: You say it. {npc} nods and goes to the Court, and the house is quiet for a long time.

events.text: The Court declines the petition, without cruelty. {npc} takes it with great dignity, in front of everyone, and cries in your arms at home. You hold {him} through the night. In the morning {he} says: 'Next age. Help me prepare.'
events.arc: A Seat in the Heavenly Court

mem.note: helped me prepare for next age

effects.log: You help. It is a long preparation, and you enjoy it more than you expected.

mem.note: suggested I give up the seat

effects.log: {npc} goes quiet. 'Perhaps,' {he} says, in a voice that does not agree.

events.text: For an age you and {npc} have shared the faithful and the offerings. This morning {he} lays plans on the table for a temple, entirely {his} own, with {his} name on the lintel and no space reserved for yours. {He} watches your face as you read.

choices.text: Say it is a fine plan

effects.log: You say so, and mean it. {npc} lets out a breath {he} had held since the morning and starts to talk about the foundations.

choices.text: Ask what is wrong with the shared temple

mem.note: asked what was wrong with ours

effects.log: 'Nothing,' {npc} says. 'Everything is wrong with it. It has your name first.' You had not noticed which came first.

choices.text: Pretend you did not see the plans

effects.log: You pretend. {npc} lets you, in a cold way, and builds anyway.

events.text: The temple needs a site, and the best sites are within the sphere of other gods. {npc} has set {his} heart on a hill with a river view, in the territory of a rival of yours. The rival has hinted that the hill could be had, for a price.

effects.log: You pay a favour, a large one. {npc} stands on the hill with the plans in hand, and cries a little.

choices.text: Tell {npc} about the price and let {him} decide

mem.note: let me decide about the hill

effects.log: {npc} considers it for a night, and decides on a plain slope with no river view. It is a good slope.

choices.text: Say the hill is not worth it

effects.log: You say so. {npc} thinks it is worth anything, and says so, and builds on a smaller hill, with a face like a closed door.

mem.note: said my hill was not worth it

events.text: The temple rises, white and plain, with {npc}'s name on the lintel in tall letters. It is a modest thing, and perfect. On the opening day pilgrims arrive. Half of them are yours. They pass under the name and keep a respectful silence.

choices.text: Bless the opening, in the background

effects.log: You bless it from a cloud, unannounced. {npc} knows by the particular quality of the light.

choices.text: Attend openly and take your seat in the crowd

mem.note: sat in the crowd at my opening

effects.log: You sit among the pilgrims, unremarkable. When {npc} sees you, there is a pause in the speech, and then a smile that carries the rest.
You skip it. {npc} does not say a word, and puts your empty seat in the family record.

events.text: The temple does not take faith from yours: that is the surprise. Pilgrims pray to both, and the two altars warm each other. A century later the joint festival of the two temples is the largest in the district. {npc} writes your name on the next lintel, small.

mem.note: wrote your name on my lintel

effects.log: You accept. It is the smallest honour you have been given, and it fills your chest for an age.

mem.note: was asked to make your name bigger

effects.log: {npc} laughs and makes it a hair bigger. It is a family joke from then on.

events.text: A scribe of the Court posts the ledger of faith for the age. {npc}'s harvest of prayers has overtaken yours, by a third. {He} says nothing. {He} does not need to. The ledger is pinned to the Court's board, where the whole of heaven can read it.

effects.log: You do. {npc} turns, startled, and sees that you are not pretending. Something in the room unclenches.

choices.text: Say the ledger measures the wrong thing

effects.log: You say it, and it sounds exactly like what it is. {npc} nods, and does not agree.
You start that afternoon. Prayers climb. {npc} sees the figures rise and works harder in turn.

events.text: The two of you have begun a quiet competition, and the faithful are the beneficiaries: rains that come on time, harvests that overflow, miracles twice a season. A third god points out, at the Court's table, that you are spoiling the mortals.

effects.log: You agree to slow, and take a season off. The mortals recover from the largesse, and you both feel rested.

ok.log: You win the season by a margin. {npc} congratulates you, graceful, and drops three notches in good humour.

fail.log: You overreach and lose the season. {npc} wins, and has the grace to look uncomfortable about it.

choices.text: Pretend you have no idea what the third god means

effects.log: The third god sighs. The competition continues with a certain new ruefulness.

events.text: A famine strikes a far country, and its people pray as one to anyone who will answer. {npc} and you both feel the pull. Whoever answers will earn a generation of faith. There is no time to confer. The pleas rise like smoke.

effects.log: You answer within the hour and take the faith. {npc} arrives a moment too late, breathless, and says nothing, and means it.
You and {npc} answer side by side, and the country prays to both. The faith is split, and the famine ends.
You step back. {npc} answers, receives the faith, and looks at you with a startled gratitude.

events.text: At the end of the age you read the ledger again. The totals are almost even. The famine country sends a joint thanks, addressed to both of you in the same hand. {npc} lays the page beside yours and smiles: 'Nobody won,' {he} says. 'Isn't it nice?'

effects.log: Nobody did. The pages are framed, side by side, in the hall of the house, where guests ask which is which.
You declare a rematch for the next age. {npc} accepts with great ceremony. Half the Court puts a stake on it.

events.text: An envoy of a rival pantheon is seen leaving {npc}'s study at dusk. {npc} does not mention it at supper. You ask, lightly, who was visiting. 'A scholar,' {he} says. It is the first small lie of the marriage, and you both hear it.

effects.log: You let it pass. The envoy returns twice that season. {npc} hides it less carefully each time.
{npc} puts down the cup. 'They want me to join them,' {he} says. 'I did not want you to hear it from a rumour.'
You follow the envoy to the border hall. The conversation you overhear is not what you feared, nor what you hoped.

events.text: The rival pantheon's terms are generous: a full seat, a domain of their own, and a place at the head of a new Lineage. {npc} lays them out for you honestly, and asks what you think. The terms are better than yours. It is plain that {he} has already weighed it.

mem.note: told me to take the rival's terms

effects.log: You say it with an open face. {npc} stares at you for a long time, then declines, and says it was a test, and that you passed it.
'I'll stay,' {npc} says. 'You only had to ask.' Both of you privately note how long you had not.
You say it as lightly as you can. {npc} nods, and the house is hushed for a week.

events.text: {npc} negotiates something cleverer than either option: a treaty of marriages between the pantheons, with {him}self as its ambassador and you as its first guest. The Court is stunned. It is a masterstroke, and it makes your house the centre of a web.

choices.text: Take up the role of first guest

mem.note: took the role of first guest

effects.log: You travel with {npc} through the rival halls and are treated as a prince. The treaty holds, at the cost of a few formal dinners.

choices.text: Decline to be the guest, but back the treaty

mem.note: backed the treaty from the house

effects.log: You stay home and back the treaty with your voice. {npc} does the travelling, and writes to you from every hall.

events.text: The treaty brings peace to a border and, to the surprise of both pantheons, a number of marriages. {npc} is remembered as a diplomat of the age. The pantheon that offered terms sends a gift: a lamp in the shape of a hand, extended. {npc} puts it on your table.

mem.note: lit the lamp of the hand with me

effects.log: You light it together. It gives a warm light, and the shadow of a hand on the wall, held out, always.

choices.text: Keep it dark, as a keepsake

mem.note: kept the lamp dark with me

effects.log: You keep it unlit. It stands on the table, a promise of light, and that is enough.

events.text: {npc} goes. Not in anger. {He} takes the seat and the domain and the Lineage that was offered, and writes to you every month. The letters are long and kind and full of the new house's small problems. The marriage endures, across a border, by courier.

effects.log: You visit, bearing a gift of your pantheon's salt. {npc} receives it ceremonially, and stays up all night talking about the new house.

choices.text: Write back, and keep the house

mem.note: was written to across the border

effects.log: You write back, once a month, for ages. It is a long, slow, devoted marriage, conducted entirely in ink.

events.text: A pilgrim stops you on the cloud road and thanks you for the miracle at the hidden shrine of the north. You have no shrine in the north. You have a strong suspicion about who does. {npc} is, at that moment, in the north, 'visiting a cousin'.
events.arc: The Shrine You Were Not Told About

mem.note: was visited at my hidden shrine

effects.log: You go. The shrine is small, new, well kept, and has both your names on it. {npc} is mending its roof, and looks up in alarm.

mem.note: was asked at supper about the shrine

effects.log: 'I was going to tell you,' {npc} says. 'Once it was a little more finished.' That is, you realise, the whole of the problem.

choices.text: Say nothing, and send a blessing north

effects.log: You send a blessing to the north, unmarked. A day later {npc} comes home with a tiny, secret smile and no explanation.

events.text: The hidden shrine is a village's creation, not {npc}'s: the villagers built it unasked, after both of you answered a prayer in the same hour. {He} has been maintaining it in secret because {he} was embarrassed. The shrine has been waiting for you.
events.arc: The Shrine You Were Not Told About

mem.note: visited the shrine openly with me

effects.log: You visit side by side. The village erupts. A feast is held. {npc} hides {his} face behind a bun, and you have to laugh.

choices.text: Leave the shrine hidden, as a private place

effects.log: You agree to keep it hidden. It becomes your place, the one that no one else in heaven knows.

events.text: Years pass. The hidden shrine, kept private, becomes something quiet and extraordinary: a place where {npc} and you hold the faith of one village is poured entirely into the pair of you. It gives you a small, steady strength, the kind that lasts.
events.arc: The Shrine You Were Not Told About

mem.note: returned to the shrine yearly with me

effects.log: You return each year on the same day. The village has forgotten why you come, and welcomes you anyway.
You tell no one, ever. It remains the best secret of the Court, kept by two gods in a village that never asks.

events.text: It happens slowly, and then at once: {npc} breaks through to a greater divinity, a full rung above you, in a single night. The Court's heralds sound the horns. Your Divine Consort stands in the doorway, lit like a sunrise, with an apologetic face.
events.arc: The Consort Who Rose Past You

effects.log: You cheer. {npc} laughs and cries and lets you spin {him} round the room. The horns are very loud.
You smile. It is a good smile, and it costs you something, and {npc} sees what it costs.

choices.text: Say the Court will make a fuss of you now

effects.log: You say it lightly, and it is true. {npc} nods, thoughtful, with a hand on the doorframe.

events.text: The Court's attention turns to {npc} like a sunflower. Invitations arrive in stacks. The heralds greet {him} first at the door. You are, for the first time, 'the consort of'. {npc} notices before you say anything, and takes your arm in the corridor.
events.arc: The Consort Who Rose Past You

effects.log: You walk in together. The heralds fumble the order, and then, after a pause, announce you both at once.

choices.text: Step back and let {him} have the hall

effects.log: You step back. {npc} turns, hurt, and says, 'Come here.' You come. The Court is not impressed with either of you.

choices.text: Stay home from the Court for a season

effects.log: You stay home. {npc} comes back each evening with the day's news and a puzzled, tender look.

mem.note: stayed home while I was feted

events.text: {npc} offers to lift you with {him}: a rite of the greater divinity, in which a consort may be carried up one rung, at some cost to the carrier. It is generous and risky. It would put you level. {He} watches your face for any trace of pride.
events.arc: The Consort Who Rose Past You

effects.log: {npc} lifts you. The cost is real, and shared. You come out of the rite level, and together, and {npc} is pale and glad.

choices.text: Refuse: you will climb by your own road

effects.log: You refuse. {npc} bows {his} head, proud and sad. 'Then I will wait on the stair,' {he} says.
'Some years,' {npc} says. 'A few. I would give them.' You do not accept, but you do not forget the offer.

mem.note: offered to pay years to lift me

events.text: A century on, you stand level, lifted or climbed, and the Court has long since stopped using the phrase 'consort of'. {npc} sits at your side at the high table and takes your hand in view of everyone. Nobody remembers who rose first.
events.arc: The Consort Who Rose Past You

mem.note: took my hand at the high table

effects.log: You take it. The table notices, and says nothing. Something in the long hall has quietly changed.

choices.text: Raise the hand, and toast the Court

mem.note: raised my hand and toasted the Court

effects.log: You raise the joined hands. The Court raises its cups, startled, and then drinks. The toast is remembered for ages.

events.text: You reach the higher rung eventually, by your own road, a long age after {npc}. The waiting {he} did on the stair is written in the Book of Fates as a deed. When you step up, {npc} is at the top with a warm cup, saying, 'You were long.'
events.arc: The Consort Who Rose Past You

choices.text: Say you were not so long

mem.note: reached the rung on your own road

effects.log: 'A few ages,' {npc} says. 'Barely a minute.' The cup is warm. The stair is quiet. You sit.
You thank {him} for the waiting, and the stair, and the cup. {npc} says that is what the cup was for.

events.text: You are called away for a season, an errand of the Court that cannot be delegated, and {npc} offers to keep your domain in your absence. It is a generous thing to offer. It is also, as you both know, a test with a very open door.
events.arc: The Consort Who Kept Your Domain

choices.text: Accept, with a list of instructions

mem.note: left me a list of instructions

effects.log: You leave a list. {npc} reads it, folds it, and says nothing. The list does not make the journey home.
You hand over the keys. {npc} takes them as if they were glass. You feel a lightness all the way up the stair.

choices.text: Decline, and delegate to a junior god

effects.log: You hand it to a junior god. {npc} bows, very politely, and the house is a trifle cool for a while.

events.text: When you return, the domain is thriving. The faithful speak well of {npc}'s keeping. {He} has made several changes, all of them good, all of them without asking. {He} stands in the hall of offerings, hands behind {his} back, awaiting your verdict.
events.arc: The Consort Who Kept Your Domain

effects.log: You praise them, one by one, and mean it. {npc} blossoms and shows you three more, and your domain has never been so well.
You reverse them within the year. {npc} notices each one and says nothing.

choices.text: Ask {him} to keep the domain again next time

effects.log: 'Gladly,' {npc} says, and you realise you have made a decision you had not meant to.

mem.note: was asked to keep the domain again

events.text: A second absence, a longer one, and this time the domain is not returned to you at once. {npc} has kept it so well that the faithful have grown to prefer {him}. You come home to a hall where the offerings bear {his} name beside yours, larger.
events.arc: The Consort Who Kept Your Domain

effects.log: You accept it. {npc} presses your hand for a full minute, grateful and overwhelmed. The domain is run by two, now.

choices.text: Ask for the old order back

mem.note: asked for the old order back

effects.log: You ask. {npc} gives it back, to the letter, and the hall's air stays thin for a decade.

events.text: Eventually {npc} moves on to another domain, leaving yours in good order. It is a cordial parting between colleagues, not a quarrel. You and {npc} keep the habit of long dinners where you discuss the faithful of both houses, plainly, as friends.
events.arc: The Consort Who Kept Your Domain

effects.log: Dinners, weekly, for an age. You solve more of the Court's problems over them than the Court does in session.
The dinners lapse, by degrees. You meet in the corridor, now and then, and nod.
